articles.title: Kurdish-led SDF announces dissolution, integration into Syrian state
articles.summary: The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) Mazloum Abdi announced the dissolution of the group on Tuesday, saying it would be fully inte...
articles.body:
The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) Mazloum Abdi announced the dissolution of the group on Tuesday, saying it would be fully integrated into Syrian state institutions.

In a press statement delivered at the presidential palace in Damascus after a meeting with transitional President Ahmad al-Sharaa, Abdi said the Kurdish Autonomous Administration in north-eastern Syria - established during the country's civil war - would also be dissolved.

Abdi said the SDF's mission had ended and that the group was moving "from the phase of defence to the phase of building Syria."

"All military and civilian formations" affiliated with the SDF and the Kurdish Autonomous Administration would also be integrated into state institutions, Abdi said.

The SDF was formally established in October 2015 and became the main US-backed force fighting Islamic State in north-eastern Syria.

The announcement represents a major step toward ending the separate military and administrative structures that Kurdish-led authorities have maintained in parts of north-eastern Syria since the fall of long-time dictator Bashar al-Assad in late 2024.

After government forces withdrew from large parts of north-eastern Syria during the 2011 uprising, Kurdish forces established control over much of the area.

Following the ouster of al-Assad in December 2024, Damascus and the Kurdish-led authorities began negotiations over the future of the SDF and the administration of north-eastern Syria.

The SDF and the Syrian transitional government signed an agreement on January 29 to integrate the force, along with the Kurdish region's security and administrative bodies, into state structures.

The step came following weeks of clashes between government forces and SDF fighters in north-eastern Syria.

"We want this day to mark a real transition: from the battlefield to the field of development, from the era of arms to the era of peace, and from defending Syria to building Syria," Abdi said on Tuesday.

Under Assad, Kurds were marginalized and faced restrictions on cultural and linguistic expression, while a 1962 census in the north-eastern Hasakah province left tens of thousands without Syrian citizenship.

Kurdish-language education was not formally recognized in state schools, a longstanding Kurdish demand.

Abdi said he had asked al-Sharaa for an open mind regarding the issue, noting that "the right to education in Kurdish is among the most fundamental rights of our Kurdish people."

articles.title: UN chief condemns Haiti gang attack that killed at least 47
articles.summary: UN Secretary General António Guterres has condemned a gang attack in Haiti that killed at least 47 people, including 22 who were reportedly executed at a chu...
articles.body:
UN Secretary General António Guterres has condemned a gang attack in Haiti that killed at least 47 people, including 22 who were reportedly executed at a church compound where they had sought shelter.

The attack took place at the weekend in Kenscoff, a community on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince.

"The relentless gang attacks on communities and the loss of lives underscore the alarming security conditions in Haiti and reinforce the urgent need to intensify Haitian and international security efforts to counter gangs," Guterres' spokesman, Stéphane Dujarric, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Guterres also reiterated his call for Haitian authorities to "ensure that those responsible for such attacks are held accountable," including through specialized judicial units recently established with international support to investigate mass crimes.

According to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH), more than 50 people were also abducted and 22 injured in Sunday night's attack on Kenscoff, around 10 kilometres south of Port-au-Prince.

The attackers targeted the centre of the community, setting numerous homes on fire and storming a church compound where displaced people had sought shelter, broadcaster Radio Télé Galaxie reported.

The UN's Dujarric said it was believed that 22 of the victims were killed at the church complex.

Police eventually managed to push back the attackers and regain control of the area.

Haiti's transitional government confirmed the attack but did not provide a death toll. It described the violence as a "heinous criminal attack," placed security forces on the highest level of alert and deployed reinforcements.

articles.title: In 1957, Georgia artist Eddie Owens Martin began transforming his inherited farmhouse and seven acres; 29 years of work created six major structures and 900+ feet of painted walls, now preserved as one of Americaâs most significant visionary art environments
articles.summary: US News: In 1957, eccentric folk artist Eddie Owens Martin returned to his rural roots near Buena Vista, Georgia, and began turning a seven-acre family propert.
articles.body: In 1957, eccentric folk artist Eddie Owens Martin returned to his rural roots near Buena Vista, Georgia, and began turning a seven-acre family property into a colourful world of painted totems, geometric designs and tall masonry walls. Over the next 29 years, Martin, who called himself "St. EOM", built six major structures and more than 900 feet of brightly painted walls. The site became what is now considered one of North America's most important visionary art environments. Known as Pasaquan, a name Martin created to mean "the past coming together", the site combines Mesoamerican designs, African patterns, Eastern symbols and futuristic ideas into a highly personal style.From fortune teller to Georgia visionaryBorn in 1908 to a family of rural Georgia sharecroppers, Martin left home for New York City at 14. He spent the next three decades working in the city's nightlife and later became a professional fortune teller. According to biographical records maintained by Columbus State University, Martin experienced powerful spiritual visions while seriously ill in 1935. He said a futuristic being told him to change his life and follow "Pasaquoyanism", a personal spiritual system that linked growing long hair with spiritual energy, harmony with the universe and artistic creation. "You're gon' be the start of somethin' new, and you'll call yourself Saint EOM, and you'll be a Pasaquoyan, the first one in the world," Martin recalled of the vision, according to statements preserved by the Pasaquan Preservation Society. After his mother's death, Martin returned to Marion County in 1957 and began building his vision on the family property. He funded the work through fortune telling and tarot readings for local residents. Without formal architectural plans, he spent decades constructing concrete buildings, circular dance platforms, two-storey pagodas and detailed shrines. "I built this place to have somethin' to identify with, 'cause there's nothin' I see in this society that I identify with or desire to emulate," Martin said in archival interviews preserved by the John Michael Kohler Arts Center.Decay leads to major restorationMartin died in 1986. Local supporters then formed the Pasaquan Preservation Society to protect the unusual site. Despite their efforts, years of extreme weather, high humidity and termite damage badly affected the painted walls and wooden structures. Pasaquan was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2008, recognising its importance as a major example of outsider art. But the site still faced serious physical damage. In late 2013, preservation leaders turned to the Wisconsin-based Kohler Foundation after deciding that a full restoration was beyond the resources available locally. The foundation took responsibility for the site in 2014 and began one of the most complex efforts to restore an American art environment. The two-year project involved specialist conservators from Parma Conservation in Chicago, International Artifacts in California and regional construction teams. Workers repaired damaged masonry foundations, treated extensive termite damage, removed overgrown vegetation and carefully repainted deteriorating surfaces. Historical photographs were used to match the bright colours and designs created by St. EOM.Preserving Pasaquan for the futureAfter the restoration was completed in 2016, the Kohler Foundation donated the seven-acre Pasaquan site to Columbus State University (CSU), securing its future as a public and educational site. Today, Pasaquan is managed through the university's Department of Art. It operates as an educational centre, museum and residency site for visiting artists from around the world. Most of St. EOM's outdoor sculptures and painted walls remain at the original site in Marion County. Some of his paintings, textiles and jewellery are also held in permanent collections at CSU and the John Michael Kohler Arts Center, helping protect his work from potential natural disasters. Pasaquan remains open for self-guided tours, educational programmes and cultural events. The colourful complex stands as a lasting record of Martin's 29-year effort to create his own alternative world from concrete, paint and personal belief.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Kentucky county closed a 225-acre golf course after it averaged only 9,000 to 10,000 rounds a year; the site is now becoming one of the countyâs largest new public parks, with 70% preserved as greenspace
articles.summary: US News: A former golf course in Kentucky is being transformed into a sprawling 225-acre public park featuring hiking and biking trails, climbing structures, a.
articles.body: A former golf course in Kentucky is being transformed into a sprawling 225-acre public park featuring hiking and biking trails, climbing structures, a dog park, interactive water features and a potential Go Ape aerial adventure course.According to the August 2026 edition of Whatâs Happening, the future New Kenton County Park in Independence is expected to break ground in 2026, marking a major new chapter for the former Fox Run Golf Course. County leaders envision the property as a destination where families can spend an entire day exploring, playing and enjoying the outdoors.âThis project has always been about creating something completely different from anything else in our region,â Kenton County Judge/Executive Kris Knochelmann said. âWe want this park to become a place where families can spend an entire day exploring, playing and making memories.âFrom golf course to 225-acre public parkLocated at 604 Independence Station Road in Independence, Kentucky, the property was once home to Fox Run Golf Course. The course averaged only about 9,000 to 10,000 rounds annually, significantly below the roughly 30,000 rounds generally considered necessary for a financially sustainable 18-hole course.In November 2019, Kenton County transitioned management of its golf courses to a third-party operator. As part of the process, officials recommended closing Fox Run to improve the long-term financial sustainability of the county's golf operations.After the closure, the county explored potential redevelopment options and hired CBRE to examine possible future uses for the broader golf course property.Officials eventually discovered that a deed restriction applied to much of the 598-acre property, including the county's other golf courses, Willows and Pioneer. Because the land had originally been acquired using Land and Water Conservation Fund dollars, it was required to remain in recreational use.Rather than leave the former golf course underutilized, the Kenton County Fiscal Court decided to preserve it as public recreational space. In August 2020, the Fiscal Court formally approved converting Fox Run Golf Course into a public park.Residents can already explore the propertyThe property is currently available for passive recreation while the larger development moves forward. Residents can hike, walk, fish, cycle, observe wildlife and explore the natural surroundings.The planned park will preserve much of that natural character. County officials expect approximately 70% of the 225-acre site to remain untouched by construction.The park's design is centered around three distinct ridges - Civic Ridge, Adventure Ridge and Trail Ridge - each offering a different type of experience.Civic Ridge will focus on familiesCivic Ridge is planned as the park's main gathering and family recreation area.The proposed amenities include improvements to the existing fishing pond, a dog park, an outdoor fitness zone, playground equipment, a shelter house and interactive nature-inspired water features similar to a splash pad.The area will provide spaces where families can gather while remaining connected to the surrounding landscape.Adventure Ridge will bring thrillsFor visitors looking for more active experiences, Adventure Ridge will feature outdoor recreation and adventure facilities.Plans include mountain bike trails, a pump track, a climbing wall, additional climbing structures and a potential Go Ape aerial adventure course.Go Ape is known for elevated obstacle courses, zip lines and treetop experiences. If the attraction is finalized, county officials say it would make the park one of only a select number of locations nationwide to offer the experience.Trail Ridge will preserve natureThe largest of the three ridges will focus on trails, exploration and access to nature.An extensive trail network will wind through the property, while interactive art installations and nature-based experiences are planned to give visitors opportunities to explore the landscape in new ways.The former fairways will therefore have a very different future from their days as a golf course, with much of the land remaining dedicated to natural surroundings and outdoor recreation.Years of planning behind the transformationThe vision for the park began taking shape in 2021, when Kenton County used grant funding to hire Human Nature to develop a comprehensive master plan.The planning process involved extensive community engagement and was divided into three stages: awareness, exploration and vision. Residents and stakeholders were invited to provide input on the site's future and the kinds of amenities they wanted to see.In August 2024, Human Nature was contracted to update the master plan, refine priorities and develop updated cost estimates.J.S. Held was selected in January 2025 as the project's owner's representative, while Bayer Becker joined the team later that year to provide design services. In April 2026, Prus Construction was selected as construction manager.The project team now anticipates breaking ground later in 2026.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Damascus condemns Israel Katz after visit with IDF soldiers on Mount Hermon
articles.summary: Katz's visit follows an IDF strike in Syria near Damascus on Saturday, which itself followed a larger strike on a military airfield on August 18. The Syrian...
articles.body:
Katz's visit follows an IDF strike in Syria near Damascus on Saturday, which itself followed a larger strike on a military airfield on August 18.

The Syrian government condemned Defense Minister Israel Katz's visit to Mount Hermon on Tuesday, Syria's Foreign Affairs Ministry said in an X/Twitter post, calling the action "illegal."

"The Foreign Affairs Ministry stresses that these hostile practices constitute a blatant provocation and a clear violation of international law and the United Nations Charter, as well as a breach of the 1974 Disengagement Agreement, which requires respect for the ceasefire lines and not crossing them," the ministry's statement read.

The ministry called upon the international community to pressure Israel into stopping its "repeated violations," withdrawing from the territory, and "respecting the sovereignty and territorial unity of the Syria."

Katz met with IDF soldiers based on Mount Hermon during his visit earlier on Tuesday, telling them that Israel "will not move from Mount Hermon and the security zone as long as there are jihadist threats to the State of Israel," according to i24 News.

"The message to the Syrian president is clear," said Katz. "When you wake up in the morning in the palace in Damascus and look up at Mount Hermon and see the IDF, you know that we are here to protect our communities and our border."

Katz emphasized the strategic significance of the territory, noting the vantage point it provides to the IDF along several fronts.

"[It overlooks] Damascus from above, 35 kilometers away, overlooking the Bekaa Valley in Lebanon, a Hezbollah stronghold from above," he was cited by i24 as saying.

IDF strikes Syrian terrorist near Damascus, military airfield in Idlib

Katz's visit follows an IDF strike in Syria near Damascus on Saturday against a terrorist in the "final stages" of preparing a terror attack against Israeli soldiers, the military said at the time.

A more significant IDF strike occured on August 18 against the Abu al-Duhur military airfield in Idlib province in northwestern Syria, with experts telling The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday that the strike sought to avoid a direct clash with Turkey amid a buildup of Turkish forces in the area.

Danielle Greyman-Kennard contributed to this report.

articles.title: The Syrian Democratic Forces, tip of the spear in anti-jihadist fight
articles.summary: The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, whose dissolution was announced by their leader Mazloum Abdi on Tuesday, were the Washington-backed de facto army o...
articles.body:
The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, whose dissolution was announced by their leader Mazloum Abdi on Tuesday, were the Washington-backed de facto army of the Kurds' autonomous administration in Syria and spearheaded the battle against jihadists.

The force was Syria's most highly trained and organised for years, until Washington dropped them for the new US-friendly authorities in Damascus.

Experts say the SDF's dissolution marks the end of an era for the country's Kurds, who had long dreamt of autonomy before the 2024 fall of Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad.

The force was formed in 2015 at the instigation of the United States, impressed by the Kurdish fighters who had defeated the Islamic State group in Kobane in the north, and seeking a reliable partner in the battle against the jihadists.

The SDF then led the battle against IS, which was defeated territorially in Syria four years later.

The force amassed around 100,000 fighters at its peak, was composed of Kurds and Arabs, and controlled swathes of Syria's oil-rich north and northeast.

But following January clashes that saw the Kurds lose large chunks of territory to government troops, the two sides signed a deal to integrate Kurdish military and civilian institutions into the state.

Arabs within their ranks also defected en masse after Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's army took control of two previously Kurdish-held provinces, Raqa and Deir Ezzor, leaving them weakened.

"Dissolving for SDF means a bitter end" for the Kurds, Mutlu Civiroglu, a Washington-based analyst and expert on the Kurds, told AFP, adding that it marked "the end of Kurdish strength in Syria".

The Kurdish force was also faced with repeated Turkish invasions between 2016 and 2019, with Ankara saying it wanted to push these fighters away from its border.

Turkey has long viewed the SDF as linked to the Kurdish militant Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which waged a decades-long insurgency in the country.

The SDF was dominated by the People's Protection Units (YPG), a Kurdish militant group seen by Ankara as an extension of the PKK.

Following a call by its jailed leader Abdullah Ocalan, the PKK formally renounced its armed struggle against Turkey in May last year, drawing a line under four decades of violence that has claimed around 50,000 lives.

The People's Protection Units denied any links with the PKK, but it was "indeed the PKK that directs the YPG behind the scenes", Syria specialist Fabrice Balanche said before the SDF dissolution.

"The YPG was formed in 2011 by PKK veterans," including SDF chief Abdi, Syria analyst Nanar Hawach of the International Crisis Group told AFP prior to Tuesday's announcement.

The January agreement with Damascus, under which Kurdish fighters would be integrated into state structures, stipulates that the SDF commit to expelling all non-Syrian PKK leaders and members from the country.

"While limited in number, they have held significant influence in command and administrative roles," Hawach told AFP, adding their numbers are estimated in the hundreds to low thousands.

In a speech earlier in August, Abdi acknowledged that "thousands of young Kurdish men and women" supported the SDF from "other parts of Kurdistan", referring to areas of Iran, Iraq and Turkey.

He also affirmed that, "at our request and according to a practical plan, those forces withdrew from here, and we can say that a new phase has begun in this region."

The SDF's integration into the state is a major victory for Sharaa, who has been trying to cement control over all of Syria since Assad's ousting.

articles.title: Dolly Parton, beloved US country music icon, dies at 80
articles.summary: Parton won worldwide acclaim for her songwriting, colorful public persona, and reputation for warmth and generosity.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, a United States country music icon who won the adoration of fans around the world with her compelling songwriting and vibrant personality, has died at the age of 80.

Parton’s publicist said in a statement on Tuesday that the famed musician had passed away peacefully in Nashville, Tennessee.

“Dolly has lived in the light, and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents, and countless others who have watched her and longed for her to meet them in the heavens,” her nephew Bryan Seaver said in a video posted on Parton’s Instagram account.

“Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians, and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent. By her example, we believed that anything was possible. She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history,” he added.

Throughout her career, Parton wrote hundreds of songs, including classics such as “Jolene”, “9 to 5”, and Coat of Many Colours”, and won a degree of acclaim and public affection that few artists in the modern era have been able to match.

With enormous blonde wigs, sparkling outfits and a self-deprecating wit, Parton became one of the best-known country music artists in the US, rising to the heights of stardom from her humble beginnings in a log cabin in the southern US state of Tennessee.

She gave her first musical performances in church, where her grandfather was a preacher, and appeared at the age of 13 at the storied country music venue the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, where she was introduced by Johnny Cash as “a little girl here from up in East Tennessee”.

Raised as one of 12 children by a father who had quit school to work on a farm and struggled with reading, she later started an education nonprofit called Imagination Library that sent free books to children across the state.

Such endeavours helped further endear Parton to the public. Fans reacted with sadness to news of her death on Tuesday, sharing anecdotes about her widespread appeal and history of personal warmth and generosity.

US President Donald Trump announced on social media that he was ordering flags to be flown at half-staff for a week in honor of Parton.

“Dolly Parton’s legacy is not celebrity, but humanity. She came from poverty to become the most important native of Tennessee,” Kyle Young, CEO of the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum, to which Parton was inducted in 1999, said in a statement. “She shared her fortunes for the good of all of us, and shared her soul in every note she sang.”

Parton was the recipient of 55 Grammy nominations and 10 wins, making her the third-most nominated woman in Grammy history.

articles.title: Tanzania's vice-president announces resignation in unprecedented move
articles.summary: Emmanuel Nchimbi is the first vice-president to quit since independence six decades ago.
articles.body:
Tanzania's Vice-President Emmanuel Nchimbi has announced he is resigning weeks after it was reported that he had fallen out with President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

The 54-year-old shared his brief resignation letter on his Instagram account, saying he wanted to respect the president's wishes. Sources in his office and the presidency confirmed the move.

Nchimbi said he would retire from public life at the end of next week - less than 10 months after being sworn in and making him the first vice-president to step down in the history of the East African nation.

He was Samia's running mate in last October's disputed presidential election, which saw hundreds killed in post-poll unrest.

The pair were sworn in last November after winning 98% of the vote.

Violent protests in the awake of voting led to the deaths of at least 500 people, according to an official enquiry .

Opposition parties and human rights groups accused the security forces of unleashing a brutal crackdown on anti-government protesters.

"I have become convinced, without doubt, that the president wants changes, and I have therefore decided to fulfil my promise," Nchimbi wrote in his resignation letter referring to the pledge he had made to Samia that he would go if she wanted another deputy.

He thanked the president and the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party for the trust they had placed in him, and to Tanzanians for their support during his time in public service.

Nchimbi said he was leaving office in accordance with the country's constitution and would continue to be a "good citizen of Tanzania".

The vice-president has made some controversial remarks in recent weeks - which may point to the possible fallout with President Samia.

Last month, he urged Tanzanians to "fight for a new constitution", arguing that there was an opportunity to secure one before 2030.

He also linked a new constitution to ways of addressing injustice, strengthening human rights, good governance and democracy.

Nchimbi previously served as secretary-general of CCM. He also held several senior positions in government, including both minister of information and home affairs, before becoming Tanzania's ambassador to Brazil and later Egypt.

articles.body: Brittany âCinnaâ Watts became emotional during her Cinnathon stream after reaching around 80,000 active Twitch subscribers on August 24. The milestone made her the most-subscribed female streamer at the time, based on active subscribers. Instead of simply celebrating, Cinna opened up about how the pressure around her work has affected her mental health. She thanked viewers and her cameraman, Rosii, for standing by her. The achievement followed weeks of growth.Brittany âCinnaâ Watts opens up after reaching 80,000 Twitch subscribersCinna reached the milestone during Cinnathon, her August streaming event that has kept her live through much of August. TwitchTrackerâs August 24 figures listed 79,231 active subscribers, including 75,191 paid active subscribers. TwitchTracker also showed 79,231 as her all-time high.A Cinnathon tracker recorded more than 75,000 new subscribers since August 1, taking her from about 5,000 subscribers at the start of the event to more than 80,000 by August 24.During the event, Cinna gained more than 100,000 Twitch followers, showing that the subscriber record was not the only sign of growth. TwitchMetrics reported an average of about 8,800 viewers across her streams during the 30-day period.On day 24, she said the attention and pressure had been affecting her mental health.âObviously, Iâm a human. Itâs ****ing with my mental health a lot, but the thing that makes it great is you guys, and I just want to say thank you so much.âShe then began crying and spoke about her work. I know Rosii puts in a lot of work, and I think I am in a constant state ofâ¦ I feel like Iâm constantly being discredited all the time, and just **** on. Iâm not a victim. articles.title: A year after Israeli strikes killed journalists at a hospital, no one has been held accountable
articles.summary: Rights groups say Israel rarely holds troops accountable for killing Palestinians, pointing to long investigations that rarely lead to prosecution.
articles.body: TEL AVIV — It’s been a year since Israeli soldiers killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and rescue workers, in a double strike on a hospital in Gaza. No one has been held accountable. Israeli officials said the target was a suspected Hamas camera on the roof of Nasser Hospital. Among those killed were Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri and Mariam Dagga, a visual journalist who worked for The Associated Press and other news organizations. Despite repeated requests by AP, the army hasn’t provided details about the investigation or a timeline for when it could be completed. Rights groups say Israel rarely holds troops accountable for killing Palestinians, pointing to long investigations that rarely lead to prosecution. As global outrage over the Aug. 25, 2025, strikes grew, the Israeli military said that in addition to taking out the camera, six of those killed were linked to Hamas, without providing evidence. But an Israeli soldier, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution, now says the military could find no evidence linking the camera, which belonged to al-Masri, to Hamas. The soldier, who was privy to discussions surrounding the military’s response, said none of the six was the intended target of the strikes. AP sent detailed questions to the military about the allegations, as well as other questions about the strikes. The military didn’t address the questions but said the incident is being examined and findings will be transferred to the Military Advocate General’s Corps to reach a verdict on whether to open a criminal investigation. It didn’t provide a timeline. The army said it would not comment on details while the incident was under review. AP reported at the time that one of the six Israel said was linked to Hamas wasn’t on the hospital’s list of casualties and two others were medical or emergency personnel. That, along with the soldier’s account, raises serious questions about Israel’s rationale for the strikes. Why did troops fail to identify the cameraman as al-Masri, even though journalists were known to film at the hospital? Why did they strike a second time, causing most of the deaths and raising accusations of a “double tap” attack on first responders, which would be a war crime? AP and Reuters released a statement Tuesday calling again for Israel to provide a full explanation of the strikes. The news organizations also called on Israel to give journalists access to Gaza to support colleagues who have covered the war from the beginning. “A year later, we remain devastated by their deaths and are still searching for answers from the Israeli authorities about what happened,” the statement read. Nasser Hospital was a vital location for journalists News agencies like Reuters and AP supplied live video footage to newsrooms around the world from the hospital, one of the few functioning in Gaza at the time. AP repeatedly informed the army that its journalists were there. The first strike killed al-Masri and another person. As other journalists, including Dagga, and rescue workers rushed up an external staircase to help the wounded and document what happened, the military struck again, killing 20. Based on footage and eyewitnesses, none was armed. In all, Israel struck the hospital four times using high-explosive tank shells. Israeli officials afterward said Hamas was using the camera to observe nearby troops. They alleged “suspicious behavior” around the camera, but the only example they gave was that a towel draped over the camera and the person filming appeared to be an effort at concealment. Al-Masri routinely covered equipment with a white cloth to protect it from the sun and dust, a common practice among journalists in Gaza and other hot climates. Last week, the army announced criminal investigations into two other high-profile attacks by its troops in Gaza — the 2024 killing of 5-year-old Hind Rajab and her family, and the 2025 killing of 15 paramedics. It cleared troops in three other attacks that killed international aid group workers. Soldier details an attempt at damage control The soldier was connected to AP through Breaking the Silence, a group founded over two decades ago by Israeli veterans that collects testimony from soldiers and is critical of Israel’s actions in the Palestinian territories. The soldier said after high-profile strikes that kill civilians without clear military purpose, army officials search for militant links among those killed. Breaking the Silence said its testimonies show there is a “retroactive incrimination process” in which Palestinians who are killed are automatically counted as militants, even when unarmed. Retroactive incrimination is used as a “near-automatic justification for every bullet, shell or missile fired, and as a tool used to avoid carrying out real investigations,” said Nadav Weiman, the group’s executive director. AP confirmed some details of the soldier’s account, which is consistent with the military’s public response. Breaking the Silence said it corroborated the account with its own sources. The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals throughout the war, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters, though it’s provided evidence for only some of its claims. Hamas security men have been seen in hospitals during the war, controlling access to certain areas. Earlier this year, Doctors Without Borders suspended some operations at Nasser Hospital for several months after patients and staff reported seeing armed, masked men roaming parts of the building. Tank shells were fired after a drone failed The soldier and a former military official with knowledge of the situation said a high-ranking army official initially approved use of a precision weapon to take down the camera, but an attempt by drone failed for unknown reasons. The former official spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to talk to the media. The division commander then approved an alternative method, said the soldier, without saying what the method was. It’s unclear who made the decision to fire tank rounds, which can cause more damage than drone strikes. Oded Ailam, former head of the counterterrorism division in Israel’s Mossad spy service, said while commanders on the ground have a degree of freedom, they don’t have a “blank check.” “If the change is significant, particularly where it may affect the risk to civilians, it must remain within the authority, rules and intent of the original order, or require renewed approval,” he said. Israeli troops have killed over 200 journalists in the war Israeli troops have killed 207 Palestinian reporters in Gaza since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack ignited the war, according to the New York-based Committee to Protect Journalists. Israel has barred foreign journalists from entering Gaza, giving Palestinian journalists a critical role. Sara Qudah, CPJ’s Middle East and North Africa regional director, said Israel has a responsibility to conduct a prompt, transparent investigation. “When journalists can be killed without credible accountability, it becomes harder and more dangerous for the press to document conflicts and for the public to know what is happening,” she said. The lack of answers has been agonizing for families. Ezz al-Din al-Masri said he doesn’t understand why his brother, Hussam, was killed. “Unfortunately, we found that the blood of journalists in Gaza is cheap … as if the rules protecting journalists do not apply,” he said. Dagga, 33, had just taken her last photos before rushing up the stairs. Whenever her father, Riyad Abu Dagga, visits her grave, he carries her phone and camera — she always had them with her. He visits her apartment near Nasser Hospital and cries. “Had any of the daughters of the soldiers been killed unjustly, they would not have stayed silent,” he said of the Israelis. “They would want to know why.”

articles.title: UN chief condemns Haiti gang attack that killed at least 47
articles.summary: UN Secretary General António Guterres has condemned a gang attack in Haiti that killed at least 47 people, including 22 who were reportedly executed at a chu...
articles.body:
UN Secretary General António Guterres has condemned a gang attack in Haiti that killed at least 47 people, including 22 who were reportedly executed at a church compound where they had sought shelter.

The attack took place at the weekend in Kenscoff, a community on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince.

"The relentless gang attacks on communities and the loss of lives underscore the alarming security conditions in Haiti and reinforce the urgent need to intensify Haitian and international security efforts to counter gangs," Guterres' spokesman, Stéphane Dujarric, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Guterres also reiterated his call for Haitian authorities to "ensure that those responsible for such attacks are held accountable," including through specialized judicial units recently established with international support to investigate mass crimes.

According to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH), more than 50 people were also abducted and 22 injured in Sunday night's attack on Kenscoff, around 10 kilometres south of Port-au-Prince.

The attackers targeted the centre of the community, setting numerous homes on fire and storming a church compound where displaced people had sought shelter, broadcaster Radio Télé Galaxie reported.

The UN's Dujarric said it was believed that 22 of the victims were killed at the church complex.

Police eventually managed to push back the attackers and regain control of the area.

Haiti's transitional government confirmed the attack but did not provide a death toll. It described the violence as a "heinous criminal attack," placed security forces on the highest level of alert and deployed reinforcements.

Criminal gangs have been trying for years to seize control of Kenscoff because of the mountainous community's strategic location, which allows control over key road connections.

Kenscoff is also close to Pétion-Ville, a comparatively affluent suburb of the capital that is home to numerous institutions, embassies and banks.

The community lies at an altitude of around 2,000 metres and, thanks to its cooler climate, is considered a relatively desirable residential area in the Caribbean country, which has been plagued by poverty and violence.

Haiti has been without a president since the assassination of Jovenel Moïse in July 2021, while an already precarious security situation has spiralled out of control.

Violent gangs control more than 80% of Port-au-Prince and have increasingly expanded into other communities, terrorizing residents, raping women and recruiting children.

According to UN figures, armed gangs killed 2,300 people in Haiti in the first five months of this year alone. More than 1,100 others were injured and almost 100 abducted.

Haiti, the poorest country in the Americas, is due to hold elections on December 13, its first since 2016.

articles.title: Australian officials allege 3M knew for 50 years its firefighting products were toxic
articles.summary: The government alleges internal company documents discussed the chemicals' ability to remain in the human body.
articles.body:
Australia's federal government says U.S. manufacturing conglomerate 3M kept selling firefighting foam for decades even though the company allegedly knew the chemicals in it could harm people, animals, and the environment.

Those allegations appear in extensive federal court papers tied to Australia's lawsuit seeking more than 2 billion Australian dollars ($1.4 billion) from 3M and its Australian subsidiary, according to The Guardian .

The accusations add to growing scrutiny of corporate decisions that can leave communities grappling with pollution long after the products themselves are gone.

Attorney General Michelle Rowland confirmed that the government was taking 3M to court over PFAS pollution connected to 28 defense bases in Australia, The Guardian reported.

The government says 3M sold aqueous film-forming foam, or AFFF, that contained PFAS "forever chemicals," which then polluted soil and water and led to major environmental and economic harm.

The court papers argue that by 1973, 3M and its Australian operations should already have understood that the products posed potential dangers.

The government alleges internal company documents discussed toxicity and the chemicals' ability to remain in the human body and also raised possible concerns about kidney function, the immune system, fertility, puberty, and infant birth weight.

The filing says that when defense personnel watched product demonstrations in 1967 and 1968, company brochures still described the foam as "non-toxic," The Guardian reported.

3M also said the products were "non-irritating" to humans, would not damage grass, were biodegradable, and were "not expected to adversely affect the ecology of receiving streams in the vicinity of [their] use."

If the government's claims are upheld, it would mean the company continued to promote a hazardous product in reassuring terms even as contamination risks spread into everyday places such as groundwater, drains, and nearby land.

PFAS are used in a wide range of industrial and household products because they resist heat, grease, and water.

However, those same qualities also make them incredibly persistent in every sense.

Many do not break down easily, which is why they are often referred to as forever chemicals.

Australia banned three key PFAS chemicals in 2025 after years of concern over health risks and environmental contamination.

One of them, PFOA, has been identified as cancer-causing in humans.

The filing says affected sites have required contaminated soil to be removed and treated, and investigations around the bases have been underway since about 2011.

When companies describe products as safe or eco-friendly while concealing environmental concerns, the fallout can last for generations, part of a broader deceptive business practice known as " greenwashing ."

The Australian government says it has already devoted substantial sums to addressing the contamination.

According to the filing, more than 214 million Australian dollars ($153 million) has gone toward investigations, monitoring, remediation, and mitigation, and over 51 million Australian dollars ($36 million) toward research and evidence gathering.

The documents also mention legal settlements worth hundreds of millions of dollars for loss and damage, according to The Guardian.

Defense began phasing out PFAS chemicals in 2004 and stopped buying 3M's AFFF in 2003.

Even so, the filing says the chemicals have continued to leach from concrete, asphalt, soil, and sediment into groundwater and surface water, suggesting cleanup will continue.

A company spokesperson said that 3M never manufactured PFAS in Australia and had stopped selling the products at issue, while defense continued to use them.

During a hearing in Melbourne, Federal Court Justice Catherine Button commented on the scale of the dispute, saying she had "never seen a claim like this," The Guardian reported.

She added that describing the case as daunting "would be an understatement."

articles.title: A British Army commander testing war robots says they aren't always the right tool for the job
articles.summary: Uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs, can present logistics, power, navigation, and control challenges for soldiers, he said.
articles.body:
A British Army commander says ground robots can be useful but come with drawbacks.

UGVs can create logistics, power, navigation, and control challenges for troops.

Ukraine shows their value may be mainly in dangerous, specialized missions that protect soldiers.

The commander of a British Army battalion tasked with experimenting with new technologies said that his unit has tested out dozens of ground robots. He concluded that they can be useful, but only for certain missions. And they come with a long list of challenges.

As Western militaries rush to absorb lessons from the war in Ukraine and integrate more uncrewed systems into their respective forces, soldiers are finding that some systems might look good on paper but aren't effective in all combat scenarios.

Ground robots , in particular, can face weight, navigation, cost, and power constraints that raise questions about when and how they should be used. In Ukraine's case, the systems have seen use in logistics operations, replacing soldiers in highly dangerous areas of the battlefield, but soldiers have also said they're not a catch-all solution.

At a recent US Army-led exercise at Fort Irwin in California, a handful of American allies and partners gathered with US forces to experiment with new systems in a simulated conflict against a near-peer adversary. The British Army's experimentation unit, the 2nd Battalion, The Yorkshire Regiment, was present for the event alongside the unit that will take over their experimentation role, the 1st Battalion Irish Guards.

During the recent exercise, Lt. Col. John Black, commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Yorkshire Regiment, told Business Insider that he and his unit have seen and tested a wide range of uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs.

"Any use case you can think of, we've tried it," he said, adding that they're not just driving it around to see how it works; rather, they are focused on "trying to employ it in a tactical scenario."

Through that experimentation, Black and his troops have encountered problems that can make UGVs difficult to use. For instance, many of the medium- to large-sized UGVs they tested required trailers or flatbed trucks to transport. Depending on how soldiers are moving and what they're carrying, that creates a logistical burden.

And once they've moved it into position, troops still have to figure out how to get it into the fight.

"Even if they've got quite long range and good speed, there's still going to be a process where you're moving them into the fight," Black said.

UGVs can also create power and refueling challenges. Depending on the system, specifically it's size, range, and capabilities, troops in the field may need to carry extra batteries, generators, or fuel — or periodically bring the robot back to a charging point.

Remote control introduces another set of problems, from maintaining a reliable connection to keeping the robot on course. The systems can also struggle with difficult terrain .

Often, their advertised range doesn't translate cleanly to real-world conditions, such as uneven ground. Obstacles "confound" most UGVs, Black said.

Whether UGVs can rely on autonomous features is a particularly thorny subject. Autonomy has become a major area of interest across uncrewed capabilities, but Black said some manufacturers have moved away from offering autonomous UGVs.

"We have seen, over the last few years, these vendors stop offering autonomous ones because it's unworkable," he said, explaining that such autonomous features can result in the system being more expensive and difficult to use.

Despite those limitations, Black said there are certain situations where he sees value, including breaches and mine removal .

Both missions are incredibly dangerous for soldiers. For that reason, militaries have been using remote-controlled technologies for breaching fortified positions and removing mines for decades. Certain UGVs coming online now could be the next evolution in that technology, but other methods could prove more practical.

Ground robots are seeing growing use in Ukraine, sometimes operating as a safer option than sending soldiers into "the kill zone" to deliver supplies and ammo. Ukraine has also used them offensively, such as driving one equipped with a gun off a drone boat in a first-of-its-kind robotic amphibious assault.

However, their growing use in that fight hasn't settled the debate on their overall usefulness. Black indicated that they might be a niche tool, most effective only in those cases where keeping a soldier out of harm's way matters most.

articles.title: Of 27 lakh âlogical discrepancyâ deletions in West Bengal, only 7 lakh appealed
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: In a new twist to the simmering controversy over the West Bengal SIR, Supreme Court was informed Tuesday that against 27-lakh odd deletions.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a new twist to the simmering controversy over the West Bengal SIR, Supreme Court was informed Tuesday that against 27-lakh odd deletions from votersâ list because of âlogical discrepancyâ only seven lakh filed appeals seeking inclusion of their names in the electoral rolls.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was informed by senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan that of total 38.1 lakh appeals filed before the SIR appellate tribunals, an overwhelming 31 lakh were filed by those who challenged inclusion of names in the rolls claiming they were ineligible to be voters in Bengal.Chunk of WB appeals was against inclusionThis was new information for SC, which was concerned by pendency of 37 lakh appeals, as 19 tribunals in last four months decided only 82,000 appeals. The new turn means 20 lakh of 27-lakh-odd voters deleted for logical discrepancy have not appealed against being struck off the rolls during the SIR.SC said a chunk of appeals was by those challenging inclusion. EC will give breakup differentiating those seeking inclusion from exclusion. Prioritising inclusion appeals would considerably reduce burden on tribunals, it said.For petitioner Prasenjit Bose from Congress, advocates Gopal Sankaranarayanan and Neha Rathi alleged that bulk of appeals for exclusion/deletion have been filed by EC in a mechanical manner against orders of judicial officers who had directed inclusion of the names and these appeals should not be heard at all.Sankaranarayanan said Kolkata and Howrah civic polls are due in Dec and at least appeals pertaining to these areas should be decided expeditiously so nobody gets disenfranchised illegally.SC said its main concern was expeditious decision on appeals of disenfranchised people. It directed EC to respond with data on appeals pending after segregating them into two categories â those seeking inclusion and those seeking exclusion of names. It asked EC to suggest a mechanism for speeding up disposal, including increasing the number of tribunals.The bench also asked EC to detail steps taken to include names of those whose appeals had been allowed. articles.title: Texas Roadhouse says claims of white employees discussing spitting in Black customers' food in a Facebook group are 'completely unfounded'
articles.summary: US News: Texas Roadhouse clapped back at the viral social media claim that its white servers were discussing spitting in Black customers' food in a private Fac.
articles.body: Texas Roadhouse clapped back at the viral social media claim that its white servers were discussing spitting in Black customers' food in a private Facebook group as a hoax and confirmed that the claims based on which diners raised boycott calls were completely unfounded. The controversy started when an unverified claim originated on Facebook, allegedly from a user warning Black diners to avoid eating at Texas Roadhouse and Logan's Roadhouse. The post alleged that a secret Facebook group boasting over 400,000 white server members existed for the explicit purpose of organizing food contamination targeted at Black customers. Specific accusations claimed that servers were licking their fingers, spitting in saliva, and touching items like the chain's famous fresh rolls before serving them.The controversy escalated as the post went viral and customers called for a nationwide boycott."We are committed to creating an environment where every guest is treated with respect and unreasonable hospitality," Texas Roadhouse officials wrote responding to the outrage. "We do not tolerate discrimination, harassment or mistreatment of any kind, and we expect our Roadies to treat every guest with dignity and care."Texas Roadhouse brought in an independent third-party cybersecurity firm to trace the origins of the post. They confirmed there was no evidence of such a 400,000-member group existing, nor any record of food-tampering incidents linked to the claim.Travis Doster, chief communications officer of Texas Roadhouse, told USA TODAY that some social media users who defamed the chain retracted their statements after it was proved to be a hoax."Thereâs no video of any of our servers," he said. "Thereâs no video of anybody saying they have evidence. Itâs very frustrating because itâs not true." He also suggested the culprit behind the post could be bots, or automated programs that make posts mimicking human engagement online. "There is zero credible evidence this is true,â he said. âThis did not happen in any of our restaurants."Viral post deleted after creating outrageThe original Facebook post was deleted. It was allegedly shared in a Facebook group called "White and proud," where a user named Nancy Smith said they worked at an unidentified Texas Roadhouse location and was in a pact with other White servers at the restaurant to contaminate the food of Black guests.The user said this had been going on for a while, or at least since the April 2025 killing of 17-year-old Austin Metcalf by Black teenager Karmelo Anthony. Anthony has been sentenced to 35 years in prison for the stabbing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: New US sanctions signal Trump desperation on Iran, experts say
articles.summary: Economic escalation is unlikely to force the Iranian government to capitulate to US demands, according to experts.
articles.body:
The United States announced new sanctions on Iran and a slew of global entities doing business with the country on Monday, in what officials have called an “economic D-Day” and officially dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast”, in an effort to force Tehran to negotiate an end to the war.

The announcement followed repeated demands by US President Donald Trump that Iranian leaders take actions like dropping their claims over the Strait of Hormuz and return to talks to end its nuclear programme.

list 1 of 3 Trump’s latest wave of Iran sanctions: Which 60 entities are targeted?

list 2 of 3 US launches Economic war on Iran

list 3 of 3 Sanctions or missiles? How Gulf will view Trump’s new Iran approach

Nearly six months into its war on Iran, the US is seeing little impact from its military operations against the country. Crucial military munitions stocks have been depleted, and important tools used to project power globally have been redirected towards Iran.

The long-term implications of the war, analysts say, have pushed the Trump administration to try economic sanctions, but these are unlikely to compel Iran into meeting the demands.

“The United States is returning to economic pressure because military force has failed to deliver the quick victory it expected,” Negar Mortazavi, senior fellow at the US-based Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera. “The ‘economic D-Day’ declaration underscores the war’s failure so far to force Iran’s surrender or achieve Washington’s political objectives.”

“On paper, the US and Iran are a huge military mismatch,” Ryan Costello, policy director at the National Iranian American Council (NIAC), told Al Jazeera. “The US caused a lot of destruction with its munitions, but so too did Iran with its missiles and drones. So it is hard to describe the war to date as anything but a catastrophic mistake.”

While the US has killed key Iranian political and military leaders, Tehran has leveraged its geography and vast arsenal of drones and missiles, striking out at key oil and gas infrastructure in a region that has depended on drawing investors by offering stability. And Tehran’s choking of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has brought pain for consumers as far away as the US, who now pay about 40 percent more at the petrol pump than before the war.

“It was a fundamental miscalculation Trump did in the outset that the threat of war will compel the Iranians to surrender,” Trita Parsi, head of the Washington, DC-based Quincy Institute, told Al Jazeera. “Instead they fought back, and they fought back very hard.”

The US supply of missile interceptors has fallen low, according to experts like those at the Washington, DC-based Center for Strategic and International Studies. In late July, the centre found it would take at least three years for the Pentagon to bring supplies back to pre-war levels. The White House has denied any such shortage exists , but analysts say the problem is very real, even if it is temporary, and the Pentagon has been forced to redirect resources away from adversaries like China.

That has included US aircraft carriers. The Pentagon has pulled a key asset away from China , dispatching the USS George Washington from Japan to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Gulf, whose sailors have been at sea for months longer than planned because of the war.

Key US bases in the region – including the Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain – have been damaged or become unsafe for use, adding hundreds of kilometres to supply lines as ships look as far away as the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia for sourcing.

“In my judgement, the US Armed Forces have probably permanently lost access to 15 Persian Gulf bases,” retired US Army four-star general Barry R McCaffrey wrote on X.

“I think it became clear the US is running out of runway on this, so the administration pivoted to what it knows best, or has perceived as effective in the past, which is these economic tools,” said Jamal Abdi, head of the NIAC. “Really, it’s a way for the administration to scale back to where it was before this war but present it as this new enhanced pressure policy.”

‘Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?’

Instead of hitting Iran and others doing business with it, Monday’s sanctions announcement turned out to be little more than yet another warning, analysts say. While the US Department of the Treasury did sanction 60 new individuals and entities from around the globe over their business with Iran, it did not include major Chinese banks or others that help Tehran sell its oil.

At least 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil exports end up in China, netting Tehran tens of billions of dollars in revenue. Ending that trade would need the US to confront China far more directly than it is willing to do. In fact, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent admitted exactly that on Monday, when he responded to a question from reporters about why the US did not immediately announce sanctions on Chinese entities long known to facilitate oil trade.

“Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent responded.

“To me, it’s more a psychological operation than an actual warfare,” Sina Azodi, assistant professor of Middle East Politics at the George Washington University, told Al Jazeera. “It will have an impact, there’s no question, and I’m sure it’s going to scare off people and affect Iran’s economy by creating more chaos and adding uncertainty … but I don’t think it will ultimately change Iranian calculations in the short term.”

Pain for the Iranian people, gain for Washington?

The new US measures seek to expand the scope of already broad restrictions against the Iranian economy, adding the possibility of secondary sanctions against non-Iranian entities dealing with sectors like digital assets, gold, technology, aviation and shipping.

Tensions with Washington have already forced Iranians to contend with things like shortages of medicine and higher fuel prices . Many of the new sectors being targeted are crucial for common Iranians looking to find ways around previous sanctions, analysts point out. Gold can help preserve wealth as the Iranian rial tumbles. Digital assets like cryptocurrencies let relatives send and receive money across borders. Airlines let Iranians visit relatives abroad, or check on loved ones inside the country.

Quincy Institute’s Parsi said he doubts new sanctions would have an impact on the Iranian government, but they will on the Iranian people.

“I think they will likely be quite impactful and painful for the Iranian people,” he said. “But translating that pain into a shift in their policy is a completely different thing.”

He pointed out that the Trump administration has long known how Tehran reacts to attempts to squeeze it economically. During his first term in 2019, Trump was engaged in an online war with Iran, and economic measures tried to exert more pressure on Tehran, prompting Iran-backed Houthi forces to hit tankers in the Gulf as well as oilfields in Saudi Arabia .

Experts say if Iran’s back is against the wall, it will retaliate.

“If the point of these sanctions is to force them to capitulate, then from what we see in the past, the Iranians would rather escalate than capitulate,” Parsi said.

The attempted use of new sanctions will end up further exposing the limits of US power in the conflict, said the Center for International Policy’s Mortazavi.

“The sanctions will deepen the economic pain facing ordinary Iranians. But years of maximum pressure have shown that economic hardship does not automatically translate into political capitulation,” she said. “If anything, this move exposes the limits of the war: Washington can continue raising the costs for Iran, but it has yet to force Tehran to change course.”

Meanwhile, the continued failure to force Iran to give up has not only made the war itself unpopular in the US, but it has also yielded the lowest approval ratings ever for Trump himself, with just 31 percent of Americans supporting the war, and 33 percent approving of the president’s performance, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.

With US midterm elections just a few months away, that is something leaders in Tehran are well aware of, said George Washington University’s Azodi.

“They calculate ahead of midterm elections in the US that the Trump administration is not going to have an appetite for more conflict,” he said. “Iran is most likely going to try to weather the storm, absorb the pain, until the Trump administration gives them a good offer.”

articles.title: Quote of the day by Aristotle: âThe man of practical wisdom aims at avoiding pain, not at attaining pleasure"
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The pursuit of pleasure is often treated as one of life's simplest goals, but Aristotle offered a more measured view of what it means to live wisely. .
articles.body: The pursuit of pleasure is often treated as one of life's simplest goals, but Aristotle offered a more measured view of what it means to live wisely. In his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle wrote: âThe man of practical wisdom aims at avoiding pain, not at attaining pleasure.â The statement appears in his discussion of pleasure, pain and self-control, where he considers whether pleasure should be treated as the highest good. Aristotle's argument suggests that practical wisdom is not simply about seeking whatever feels good in the moment. Instead, it involves understanding which desires are worth following and recognising when the pursuit of pleasure can ultimately create greater difficulties. His words remain relevant because modern life constantly encourages people to seek comfort, entertainment and immediate satisfaction. The quote offers a reminder that wisdom can sometimes mean choosing what prevents unnecessary pain rather than constantly pursuing what feels pleasurable.Quote of the day by Aristotle: What did Aristotle mean by the quote?Aristotle's statement centres on the difference between practical wisdom and the pursuit of immediate pleasure. In Nicomachean Ethics, he discusses the way people respond to pleasure and pain and examines the behaviour of those who lack self-control. His point is not that all pleasure is bad or that a wise person should live without enjoyment. Instead, Aristotle distinguishes between pleasures that are beneficial and excessive or misguided pleasures that can lead to problems. The practically wise person therefore does not make pleasure the sole objective. Such a person understands that avoiding unnecessary pain can be more important than chasing temporary enjoyment.The idea becomes clearer when considered alongside Aristotle's broader discussion of self-control. He argues that people can become overly driven by pleasurable things and that this pursuit can itself produce pain. Someone who constantly seeks immediate gratification may eventually face consequences that outweigh the original pleasure. Practical wisdom therefore requires judgement. It means considering where a particular choice will lead rather than evaluating it only by how enjoyable it feels in the present. Aristotle's message is ultimately about moderation, foresight and the ability to place short-term desires within the context of a larger and more balanced life.Why avoiding unnecessary pain can be a form of wisdomPeople often associate wisdom with achieving more, gaining more or experiencing more pleasure. Aristotle's observation presents another way of looking at it. Sometimes the wiser decision is the one that prevents avoidable problems from developing in the first place. A person may choose discipline over excess, restraint over impulse or preparation over convenience because these choices can reduce difficulties later. This does not mean avoiding every challenge. Some difficulties are necessary for growth, and Aristotle's wider philosophy places considerable importance on developing good character through practice and habit. The point is to distinguish between worthwhile difficulty and unnecessary suffering. Practical wisdom helps a person recognise that difference and make choices accordingly.This idea remains relevant in everyday decisions. Eating or spending excessively may provide immediate pleasure but create problems later. Avoiding difficult responsibilities may feel comfortable in the moment but increase stress over time. Similarly, constantly choosing entertainment over meaningful work can offer short-term satisfaction while making long-term goals harder to achieve. Aristotle's argument encourages people to look beyond the immediate emotional reward and consider the consequences of their choices.Why chasing pleasure does not always lead to happinessAristotle's discussion is particularly interesting because he does not simply argue that pleasure is worthless. In Nicomachean Ethics, he examines different arguments about pleasure and ultimately treats pleasure as having an important place in human life. His concern is with the assumption that every pleasurable experience should automatically be pursued. Some pleasures can be excessive, harmful or connected to desires that undermine self-control.This distinction is important in a world where instant gratification is increasingly accessible. Entertainment, shopping, food, social media and other forms of stimulation can provide immediate rewards with very little effort. Yet the fact that something is enjoyable does not necessarily mean that pursuing more of it will improve a person's life. Aristotle's idea encourages a more deliberate approach. Instead of asking only whether something feels good, a person can also ask whether it is good for them, whether it supports their goals and whether the consequences are worth the temporary pleasure.Aristotle and the importance of practical wisdomPractical wisdom, or phronesis, occupies an important place in Aristotle's ethical philosophy. It concerns the ability to deliberate well about how to act in particular circumstances. Rather than relying on simple rules, practical wisdom involves judging what is appropriate in a given situation and choosing actions that contribute to a good life. Aristotle's discussion of pleasure and pain forms part of this wider examination of human behaviour, virtue and self-control.The quote therefore should not be interpreted as a simple instruction to avoid discomfort at all costs. A wise person may willingly accept temporary pain or difficulty when it serves a worthwhile purpose. Studying can be difficult, exercise can be uncomfortable and achieving an important goal can require sacrifice. The wisdom lies in understanding which difficulties are meaningful and which forms of pain are simply the consequences of poor choices. Aristotle's approach asks people to think beyond immediate feelings and consider the broader consequences of their actions.The timeless lessonAristotle's words ultimately encourage a more thoughtful relationship with pleasure and pain. A good life is not necessarily one in which every moment is comfortable or every desire is satisfied. Wisdom involves knowing when to pursue something, when to exercise restraint and when avoiding a particular choice can save us from greater difficulties later. The quote reminds us that self-control is not about rejecting pleasure but about refusing to let pleasure control our decisions. In a culture increasingly focused on instant gratification, Aristotle's ancient observation offers a simple but powerful lesson: sometimes the wisest choice is not the one that promises the greatest pleasure, but the one that prevents unnecessary pain and helps us live with greater balance and judgement.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Best hiking trails near Scott Stadium in Charlottesville: a guide for Virginia football fans
articles.summary: Before the Cavaliers kick off at Scott Stadium, explore Humpback Rocks, the Blue Hole swimming spot, and Shenandoah National Park all within 35 minutes.
articles.body: Week 0 | NC State at Virginia | Saturday, Aug. 29 | Scott Stadium, Charlottesville, VA | 3:30 p.m. ET Funny how things work out. This game was supposed to be college football's first trip to South America, with NC State and Virginia set to kick off Week 0 at Nilton Santos Stadium in Rio de Janeiro. Then the whole thing fell apart this summer when Athlete Advantage (the event organizer) told the ACC it simply couldn't pull it off. So the Wolfpack and Cavaliers got rerouted back to the far less exotic — but far more practical — Blue Ridge foothills of Charlottesville instead. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Virginia's loss of a trip to Rio is your gain. Instead of fighting for a spot on a flight to Brazil, you can be standing on a mountaintop overlooking the Shenandoah Valley by 9 a.m. and in your tailgate spot by 1. Charlottesville sits right up against the Blue Ridge Parkway and the edge of Shenandoah National Park, which means some of the best hiking in Virginia is closer to Scott Stadium than most fans realize. Here's where to go — all within an hour of kickoff and none requiring a passport or conversational Portuguese. Saunders-Monticello Trail 10 minutes from Scott Stadium | Easy The one to bring the whole crew, including grandparents and strollers. A 4.4-mile out-and-back on packed gravel and raised boardwalk, climbing gently through forest canopy up to the visitor center at Thomas Jefferson's Monticello. Dog-friendly, wheelchair-accessible and shaded most of the way. If anyone in your group wants to actually tour the house, that's a separate ticket — $23 to $30 for adults, $10 for kids 5 to 11 — but the trail itself is free. Blue Ridge Tunnel 30 minutes from Scott Stadium | Easy A change of pace from the usual mountain-view hike: a 4.6-mile out-and-back through an actual 1850s railroad tunnel carved straight through the mountain under Rockfish Gap. Bring a flashlight or headlamp — it gets really dark in there, and the temperature drops the deeper you go, which is an added bonus. BEAT THE HEAT: HERE ARE SOME OF THE BEST TIPS TO AVOID HEATSTROKE DURING A HIKE THIS SUMMER Shenandoah National Park (Rockfish Gap entrance) 25 minutes from Scott Stadium | $30 per vehicle | Moderate If you're only going to spend money on one thing this weekend besides the game, this is the one worth it. The Rockfish Gap entrance drops you right onto Skyline Drive, with two standout hikes an easy detour apart: Calvary and Chimney Rocks at milepost 90, a short trek out to a flat-topped rock overlook, and Turk Mountain at milepost 93.5, which delivers rock scrambles and real mountain views for the effort. Being a national park, it will cost you an entry fee of $30 per vehicle, which is good for seven days. Sugar Hollow Reservoir & the Blue Hole 35 minutes from Scott Stadium | Moderate The pick if you’re looking to do a little soaking. A 3-mile out-and-back from the Sugar Hollow parking area leads to the Blue Hole, a genuinely beautiful swimming hole on the Moormans River. This spot keeps showing up on the "best swimming holes in Virginia" lists for a reason. Bring water shoes; the rocks get slick. If your crew wants more of a workout instead, a separate 4.6-mile route from the same lot heads out to Big Branch Falls through a shaded forest. Humpback Rocks 30 minutes from Scott Stadium | Moderate-strenuous The payoff hike, and the one most worth setting an alarm for. It's a brutal, steep mile straight up, but the reward is a 360-degree view across the Shenandoah Valley and Blue Ridge that's tough to beat anywhere in the state. This is the one hike on the list with zero shade at the top, so this is the one to knock out at sunrise, not after brunch. Sunrise at Humpback is a bucket-list item for many UVA students. Crabtree Falls 60–75 minutes from Scott Stadium | $3 day-use fee | Moderate-strenuous Crabtree Falls is a series of five major cascades tumbling a total of 1,200 feet down the mountainside. For context, that's taller than the Eiffel Tower. And the longest single cascade in that series drops 400 feet, enough to make Crabtree Falls the tallest single vertical-drop waterfall east of the Mississippi. The hike up alongside it is a 3-mile round trip with switchbacks and handrails at the steeper spots. It's genuinely one of the most photographed trails in Virginia. The catch: this one runs 60 to 75 minutes from Scott Stadium depending on route and traffic. If you're rolling into Charlottesville just for the game, Crabtree probably isn't the move. But if you're making a weekend of it and have an extra day before or after, it's worth the drive. We should probably also mention there's another Crabtree Falls off the Blue Ridge Parkway in North Carolina. Make sure you're plugging the right one into your GPS. Truthfully, you can't go wrong no matter which trail you choose. Between the Blue Ridge Parkway, Shenandoah National Park and a reservoir system that seems to have a trail wrapped around every corner of it, Charlottesville is about as good as it gets for outdoor adventurers who also happen to love college football. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Seeking two years to frame creamy layer criteria for OBCs, Centre Tuesday requested Supreme Court for an early hearing on its application against retrospective implementation of SCâs March 11 judgement, which disallowed this classification of OBC candidates based on the salaries of parents employed in PSUs or the private sector.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta requested a bench led by CJI Surya Kant to list the application seeking certain clarifications on the March 11 judgement in the Rohit Nathan case.
