articles.title: How Nathan Straus transformed philanthropy and helped make pasteurised milk the safer choice for children
articles.summary: US News: Long before pasteurised milk became a routine part of American life, families in New York faced a serious and often overlooked public-health danger, c.
articles.body: Long before pasteurised milk became a routine part of American life, families in New York faced a serious and often overlooked public-health danger, contaminated milk. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, raw milk could carry harmful pathogens and was especially dangerous for infants and young children. One wealthy businessman, Nathan Straus, used his fortune and business experience to tackle the problem in an unconventional way. Rather than simply donating money to charities, Straus created a system that combined philanthropy with practical retail distribution. He established milk laboratories and depots where pasteurised and refrigerated milk could be sold cheaply or provided free to families who could not afford it. His campaign eventually helped push pasteurisation into mainstream public-health policy and left a lasting mark on how Americans understood safe milk.Nathan Straus turned his business experience towards philanthropyNathan Straus was born in 1848 and became wealthy through his involvement with major New York department stores, including Abraham and Straus and R.H. Macy and Co. After building his fortune, he and his wife, Lina Gutherz Straus, increasingly devoted their attention to philanthropic causes. The New York Public Libraryâs papers document his work in public health, milk pasteurisation, tuberculosis prevention and assistance to people affected by poverty and disasters. Strausâs approach to charity differed from the traditional model of simply handing out money. During the economic depression of the 1890s, he used his experience in merchandising to establish depots near New Yorkâs poorer neighbourhoods, where essential goods could be provided at reduced prices. This practical approach later shaped his campaign for safer milk. His interest in milk became particularly personal and urgent. At the time, milk could spoil during transportation and storage, while contaminated supplies could expose children to dangerous diseases. Straus believed that improving the way milk was processed and distributed could save lives.The milk crisis that put children at riskIn New York City during the 1890s, infant mortality was extraordinarily high. Raw milk was considered one of the major risks because it could contain disease-causing organisms, including bacteria associated with tuberculosis. Although scientists already understood that heating milk could destroy harmful microorganisms, pasteurisation was not yet universally accepted. Straus became one of its most determined advocates. In 1892, he established the Nathan Straus Pasteurized Milk Laboratory in New York at his own expense. The facility produced safer milk and helped establish a distribution network designed specifically to reach families in poorer parts of the city. His milk depots did more than sell a product. They made pasteurised and refrigerated milk accessible to people who might otherwise have had little choice but to purchase cheaper, potentially unsafe supplies. Some milk was sold below wholesale prices, while families unable to pay could receive it without charge. The NYPL collection includes records of the laboratory and its milk depots, including reports, brochures, instructions for mothers, infant-formula recipes and even coupons that could be redeemed at the depots.âRetail givingâ made philanthropy practicalStrausâs method has since been described as a form of âretail givingâ because it applied the efficiency of business to a social problem. Instead of creating a conventional charity dependent entirely on handouts, he developed a system capable of producing, pricing and distributing a health-protective product on a large scale. The approach also included education. Information was provided to mothers about infant care and the safe handling of milk, while doctors and nurses were involved in advising families. Straus supported efforts to demonstrate that pasteurisation could protect children without sacrificing the nutritional value of milk. His work expanded well beyond New York. According to historical accounts of his philanthropy, Straus and his wife ultimately helped establish hundreds of milk stations across numerous American cities. The NYPL collection records his efforts to promote pasteurisation through speeches, articles, medical and public-health meetings, and advocacy for legislation. The strategy was significant because it connected individual access to safer milk with a broader public-health campaign. Families could obtain pasteurised milk immediately, while policymakers and health professionals were exposed to evidence supporting wider adoption.From a private campaign to a public-health standardStrausâs campaign unfolded at a time when public-health officials were increasingly concerned about infant mortality and infectious disease. His work helped demonstrate the practical benefits of making pasteurised milk available to communities that needed it most. The wider movement eventually contributed to changes in public policy. By the early 20th century, pasteurisation was gaining much greater acceptance among American health authorities, and governments increasingly moved towards requiring safer milk supplies. Straus did not single-handedly make American milk safe, but his efforts formed an important part of a much larger public-health transformation. His particular contribution was showing that philanthropy could operate at the point where a public-health problem actually affected people's daily lives: the purchase and consumption of food.A forgotten legacy in American public healthNathan Straus died in 1931, but the records preserved his legacy is striking because the solution he promoted now seems ordinary. Today, consumers generally expect commercially sold milk to have undergone safety controls that were far from universal when Straus began his campaign. What made his philanthropy distinctive was its practical focus. He did not simply ask how much money could be donated to a cause. He asked how a wealthy businessman could use the systems of production, distribution and retail to make a basic necessity safer and more affordable. That approach helped transform milk from a potential source of serious disease into a much safer staple for American families. In doing so, Straus showed how targeted philanthropy could influence not only individual lives but also the development of public-health practices that eventually reached far beyond the people his original milk stations served.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Dolly Parton through the years, in photos: From ‘9 to 5’ secretary to ‘Hannah Montana’ godmother
articles.summary: Until she died Tuesday at age 80, Dolly Parton was the beloved Queen of Country music.
articles.body: Dolly Parton craved the camera. And until she died Tuesday at age 80, the Queen of Country’s life unspooled in photograph after photograph, turning the poor little girl with the angelic voice from eastern Tennessee into one of America’s most beloved — and recognizable — figures. It was country singer Porter Wagoner who first introduced Parton to a wider audience when he invited her in 1967 to appear on his hit TV show. By 1974, Parton was out on her own, and her signature public image — the blond wigs, the cleavage-baring outfits that showed off her hourglass figure — was cast in stone. Soon Hollywood beckoned, and Parton took it by storm, winning a Grammy for her single “Here You Come Again” and appearing in a string of hit movies that eventually earned her a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1984. Bubbly and witty, Parton was also a must-book guest on the small screen: She made more than 400 television appearances, performing on variety shows hosted by the likes of Cher and Mac Davis, and charming late-night and daytime hosts ranging from Johnny Carson and his successor, Jay Leno, to Oprah Winfrey and Conan O’Brien. Parton also hosted not one, but two TV variety shows, both called “Dolly,” which millions of Americans tuned in to watch. And in 1989, she even took a turn at hosting “Saturday Night Live,” where, during the opening monologue, the running gag was her cracking jokes while the cameraman was unable to focus on anything but her bosom. Her duets with performers ranging from Elton John and Kenny Rogers to Miley Cyrus spanned the generational divide; she became the rarest of performers — one whose fan base expanded as she grew older. With the acclaim came the awards, the invitations to give commencement speeches, the honorary degrees, the chance to perform before thousands of fans at big-time sports events. But there was a part of Parton’s life she mostly kept hidden from America’s prying eyes, the part she is said to have cherished most — her nearly 59-year marriage to her husband, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025. Dean almost never appeared in public with his famous wife and, as a result, there were very few photos of them together available to the public. And they were fine with that. “I’ve kept [my marriage] very personal and sacred and I try to keep my husband out of the business,” she said in an interview. “That’s not what he chose to do, he just happened to love me and I love him enough to not expose him to it.”

articles.title: US lawmakers urge Trump team to free American student held by Israel
articles.summary: Congress members call on Marco Rubio to ‘use every tool’ at his disposal to secure release of 20-year-old Sama Safi.
articles.body:
More than 40 members of the United States Congress have penned a letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling on him to push for the release of Sama Safi, a 20-year-old US citizen who has been detained by the Israeli military since June.

The legislators warned on Tuesday that the Palestinian American student's health is deteriorating "under appalling conditions" in Israeli custody.

"Every day that Sama remains wrongfully detained in these inhumane conditions, she is at greater risk of irreversible and life-threatening repercussions," the lawmakers, led by Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib , wrote to Rubio.

"Her life is at risk on your watch. We urge you to act swiftly and use every tool at your disposal to secure the immediate release of Sama Safi so that she can receive the medical care she urgently needs and return to her family, her studies, and the life and freedom that every 20-year-old deserves."

Six US senators – including Elizabeth Warren, Bernie Sanders and Chris Van Hollen – signed on to the letter alongside dozens of members of the House of Representatives.

Israeli forces abducted Safi, who was attending Birzeit University, from her home in the occupied West Bank in a predawn raid nearly three months ago, and they have been holding her without charge.

Safi was one of four young women who were detained as part of an Israeli crackdown on anti-occupation activism in June.

Israel has received about $25bn in US military aid since the start of the genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.

Over the past years, Israeli soldiers and settlers have killed several US citizens, including Sayfollah Musallet , who was beaten to death in a settler attack last year.

In February, Israeli settlers also fatally shot 19-year-old American citizen Nasrallah Abu Siyam. In 2024, the Israeli military killed Aysenur Ezgi Eygi , a US activist from Seattle.

None of the incidents have resulted in criminal charges against the perpetrators.

Israel detained American teenager Mohammed Ibrahim for nine months last year and only released him after an outcry from US lawmakers, as his family warned that the boy may die from malnutrition and mistreatment in Israeli custody.

Rights groups have documented horrific and widespread abuses against Palestinian detainees by Israel, including sexual violence.

"Emergency measures introduced after 7 October 2023 exposed Palestinian detainees to torture, potentially unlawful deaths, incommunicado detention, and degrading conditions," Alice Jill Edwards, the United Nations special rapporteur on torture, said in a report in May.

In their letter to Rubio, the US lawmakers underscored that Safi suffers from a chronic medical condition known as Familial Mediterranean Fever, a genetic disorder that causes fevers and inflammation, but she has not had regular access to her medication.

The Palestinian American detainee has also been moved across several facilities.

"She describes being subjected to repeated verbal abuse and being placed in painful stress positions, as well as the presence of rapidly spreading infectious skin disease, rats, and mattresses reeking of feces," the letter said.

Trump administration 'aware' of the case

The State Department said it does not comment on congressional correspondence, and it declined to comment on the specifics of Safi's case, citing privacy concerns.

A State Department spokesperson told Al Jazeera that the administration of President Donald Trump "has no higher priority than the safety and security" of US citizens.

"We are aware of reports of an American detained in the West Bank," the spokesperson said. "The Trump Administration takes its commitment to assist Americans abroad seriously and we are tracking the situation. When Americans are detained abroad, the Department advocates for their access to adequate medical care, proper treatment, and regular consular visits."

Raed Jarrar, advocacy director at the US-based rights group DAWN, suggested Safi's detention should trigger suspending American military aid to Israel under Washington's regulations, including the Leahy Law.

"Sama Safi is an American citizen. Her own government has abandoned her," he told Al Jazeera. "The State Department's job is to fight for her release, and it is refusing to do that job. US law demands more than advocacy. Under the Foreign Assistance Act and the Leahy Law, prolonged detention without charge is a gross violation of human rights, and Washington must cut all military aid to the Israeli units responsible for holding her."

The Israeli government did not respond to Al Jazeera's request for comment by the time of publication.

Earlier this month, the Israeli military told Florida radio station WMNF that it detained four "female suspects" in the West Bank "after promoting hostile terrorist activity and additional terrorist-related activities".

articles.title: Massive fishing boat runs aground at popular beach with 1,000 gallons of diesel on board
articles.summary: A 58-foot fishing boat ran aground at North Beach in Northern California's Point Reyes National Seashore, triggering a closure and diesel removal effort.
articles.body: A 58-foot fishing boat ran aground at a popular Northern California beach — prompting a closure as crews worked to remove roughly 1,000 gallons of diesel from the vessel. The Lake Bay became stranded early Friday at North Beach in Point Reyes National Seashore, according to an alert from the National Park Service (NPS). The boat was carrying 40,000 pounds of squid at the time, Inverness resident Richard James told the Point Reyes Light, a local newspaper, citing a conversation with the vessel's skipper. TSUNAMI OF SEWAGE FROM MEXICO BARRELS TOWARD US COASTLINE, OFFICIALS WARN As crews began responding to the grounding, the park service announced the temporary closing of North Beach and North Beach Road. No injuries, fuel leaks or impacts to wildlife were reported, the agency said. Fox News Digital reached out to the NPS for further comment and details. The Lake Bay can hold up to 2,800 gallons of fuel. It was reported to have approximately 1,000 gallons of diesel on board, according to a press release from the U.S. Coast Guard. Crews were coordinating with the party responsible for the vessel and a contracted salvage company to remove the fuel, the Coast Guard said. 75-FOOT BOAT SURFS WAVE, RUNS AGROUND IN HAWAII Capt. Jack Moran, owner of Sea Tow Cape May in New Jersey, told Fox News Digital that access and timing can pose challenges when dealing with a grounded vessel.  "The biggest thing is going to be accessibility," Moran said, noting that crews have to contend with tides, currents and changing conditions. "Time is the enemy. You want to try and get it off there as quickly as possible." (He is not connected to or involved with the Lake Bay fishing boat.)  With 40,000 pounds of squid reportedly onboard, Moran said removing the catch could present another challenge. "Moving a product like that is challenging at a dock, let alone removing squid from a boat on a beach," he said. For the Coast Guard, safety and environmental concerns remained at the center of the response. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Our top priorities are ensuring the safety of the first responders and the public, stabilizing the incident, and limiting environmental impacts," Lt. Cmdr. Carey Lewis, the Coast Guard incident commander, said in the release.  "Responders are continuously monitoring and evaluating the site for pollution and any potential risk factors so we can approach operations with [an] intention to minimize environmental impacts." "Our top priorities are ensuring the safety of the first responders and the public." The National Park Service asked visitors to stay away from North Beach while the closure is in effect to allow first responders to work safely. The cause of the grounding remains under investigation, the Coast Guard said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Fox News Digital previously reported on another grounding in April involving a small cruise ship near Monuriki Island in Fiji, where the Tom Hanks movie "Cast Away" was filmed. The Blue Lagoon Cruises vessel struck a reef after worsening weather caused its anchor to drag. A high-speed ferry arrived around dawn to assist with the evacuation, allowing all passengers and non-essential crew members to leave the stranded ship with their belongings. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Passengers were taken back to Port Denarau, where the cruise line arranged hotel accommodations and alternative activities. No injuries were reported among passengers or crew. Jessica Mekles of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

articles.title: Two unvaccinated people in Pennsylvania are first measles-related deaths in US this year
articles.summary: Pennsylvania reported two deaths related to measles as an outbreak there approaches 400 cases, the state Department of Health said Tuesday. Both were unvacci...
articles.body:
Pennsylvania reported two deaths related to measles as an outbreak there approaches 400 cases, the state Department of Health said Tuesday. Both were unvaccinated.

These are the first US deaths related to measles reported in 2026 and the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years.

"My deepest sympathies are with the loved ones who are facing this unimaginable loss," Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen said in a statement. "As a physician, I want to make sure that people understand that the MMR vaccine is safe and provides the best protection we have against measles."

The deaths come as US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has led efforts to make sweeping changes to federal vaccine recommendations, including those involving the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine. During Kennedy's time in office, vaccination rates have continued to fall nationwide, leaving more children vulnerable to preventable illness.

In 2021, Kennedy – who was then leading the anti-vaccine organization Children's Health Defense – visited Lancaster County, where he made light of his own childhood case of measles and stoked fears in vaccines, which he suggested were causing autism and autoimmune diseases.

On Tuesday, Kennedy called Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro to offer federal staff to help with the measles response, but Shapiro said he declined because he thought the state could manage with its own resources. He said he also told Kennedy that the disinformation he spread about vaccines was having repercussions.

"There's real-life consequences to spreading misinformation. There's real-life consequences to scaring people and not relying on actual doctors and actual medical professionals to provide unbiased information to parents so that we can make reasonable decisions for our kids," Shapiro said in a news briefing.

"Sharing conspiracy theories and misinformation does not help the cause of public health, and it leaves people less healthy and less safe, and it leaves parents in a position where it's harder for us to do our jobs to protect our children," he added.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said on social media that it "is working closely with state and local health departments to strengthen response efforts, rapidly support affected communities across the state, and communicate the steps people can take to slow the spread of measles. The MMR vaccine provides the most effective protection against measles and helps prevent its spread. CDC will continue to follow Pennsylvania's lead and provide resources to support the state's response."

Both of the Pennsylvania deaths were in residents of Lancaster County. Health officials said they will not release any additional details.

Pennsylvania has confirmed 393 measles cases in 28 counties in 2026, Bogen said in a news conference Tuesday. Roughly half of them have been in Lancaster County, she said.

About 20% of cases in Pennsylvania this year have required hospitalization. Among measles cases confirmed by the health department, none have been in people who have received both recommended doses of the MMR vaccine, she added.

The highly contagious virus has continued its historic resurgence in the US this year, with a second record-breaking year in a row. The country has recorded more cases than 2,700 cases this year, more than any other year since 1991 – surpassing a grim milestone that was just topped last year.

The disease was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, but more cases have been recorded in the past year and a half than there have been in the previous 25 years combined. Experts expect that the US will soon lose its elimination status, the recognition by the World Health Organization that measles is no longer transmitting regularly within a country.

Early symptoms of measles include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, Pennsylvania health officials said, and a rash follows a few days later, starting on the head and spreading downward. Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure.

Measles can spread when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes, and the virus remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the person with infection leaves the area.

Measles can cause serious short- and long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling. Death related to measles are rare but happen in 1 to 3 patients per 1,000 cases.

"People have forgotten how serious it can be, especially for the very young, the pregnant and the very old," Bogen said.

Two doses of the MMR vaccine are 97% effective against measles. Pennsylvania health officials are recommending early or catch-up MMR doses for people as young as 6 months who aren't fully protected.

"These deaths are entirely preventable," said Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center and an infectious disease physician at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia.

Last year, the US reported its first measles deaths in decades, including two unvaccinated children in Texas.

articles.summary: India News: National Medical Commission (NMC) is seeking to re-register around 11 lakh doctors to create an updated national medical registry, yet it has failed t.
articles.body: National Medical Commission (NMC) is seeking to re-register around 11 lakh doctors to create an updated national medical registry, yet it has failed to register even fresh entrants to the profession despite many state registries sharing records every year, reports Rema Nagarajan.Based on MBBS seats and pass rates, at least 68,000 new doctors should have registered to practice, but only 44,400 entries were recorded in 2025 with at least 24,000 graduates missing in Indian Medical Register. The gap points to potential failure of NMC to sync state and national registries, as required under NMC Act.NMC pushes old docs to re-register, but canât net new onesThe National Medical Commission (NMC) is pushing a regulation to make about 11 lakh doctors re-register to create an updated national medical registry, but it has failed to even register fresh entrants to the profession despite many state registries sending it new entries every year.With over 91,000 MBBS seats available in 2020-21, even with an estimated 75-90% pass percentage, at least 68,000 MBBS graduates should have registered to practice in 2025. Yet the Indian Medical Register shows just over 44,400 entries. That means at least 24,000 of those who graduated just last year are missing from the registry.If thousands of foreign medical graduates who register each year are included, the number of freshly minted doctors missing from the registry would be even more. For instance, in 2023, over 10,000 foreign medical graduates passed the qualifying exam, after which they have to complete a mandatory one-year internship before receiving permanent registration that would make them eligible to practice in India. So, most of these 10,000 would have registered in 2025. Thus, the total number of doctors registering in 2025 would be roughly 80,000, but just over half the number (55%) have been added to the registry.Most of the doctors would have registered with state medical councils. However, new entries in state medical council registries are not being reflected in the national registry as the NMC is yet to synchronise all state registries with the national registry. The NMC Act, 2019, had mandated such synchronisation. It is yet to happen, almost six years after the NMC was constituted in Sept 2020. Neither is NMC adding the new entries that many state councils send every year.Take Assam Medical Council, for instance. It is a state with only govt medical colleges. In the national registry, there are a total of 25,722 registrations from the state council. It shows only one entry for 2025, zero for 2024 and 2023, 106 entries for 2022 and 353 in 2021. The website shows 890 registered in 2024. There were over 720 seats in Assam in 2015 and 1,000 seats in 2020. How is NMC accepting zero entries in 2023 and 2024, or only 106 in 2022?Similarly, NMCâs registry has a total of 67,142 entries from Kerala with just seven entries in 2025 and 17 in 2024. In 2014, Kerala had 3,650 MBBS seats, which increased to 4,500 by 2020. âWe are sending details every year... In the name of a new updated NMR, they are not updating the existing one,â said KSMC chief Dr Harikumaran Nair.If the NMC were to register only those who became doctors in the last five years, including foreign medical graduates, it would have had an updated registry of over 3.5 lakh doctors (32%) of the estimated 11 lakh who are said to be available.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: New mom woke to find baby "blue and cold"—She knew exactly what to do
articles.summary: A Missouri mom describes the horrifying moment she found her newborn unresponsive and sprang into action.
articles.body:
A new mom has described the moment she woke up to find her newborn daughter "blue and cold" and what she did next.

Layna Wells, of Missouri, said there was nothing out of the ordinary about that particular morning. She woke up at 5 a.m. to feed her 3-week-old daughter, Stevie, burped her, and held her for about 15 to 20 minutes before laying her back down to sleep.

Wells said it was around 7 a.m. when she next woke to every new parent's worst nightmare.

"I don't know why I woke up, but I did," she told Newsweek . "I rolled over to see my daughter blue and cold."

Unswaddling Stevie's limp, blue body, Wells immediately sprang into action.

"I immediately turned her over, did the five blows between the shoulders, turned her over again and did the compressions," she said.

That was when she noticed Stevie had started to breathe again.

"I started to aggressively massage her skin to make sure the blood was flowing properly, and that's when her eyes opened," Wells said. "She didn't cry."

Wells said Stevie was awake all the way to the ER but "never cried" during the journey.

"When they started checking her vitals and took her temperature, that's when she started to cry for the first time since CPR, and that was well over an hour later," Wells said.

She was diagnosed with a Brief Resolved Unexplained Event (BRUE).

A BRUE is a brief, unexplained episode in an infant that has resolved by the time medical care is sought. While the event can be frightening for parents, modern pediatric guidance views BRUE as distinct from Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) and Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID), and most infants who experience a low-risk BRUE have excellent outcomes and are not at increased risk of sudden infant death.

Historically, a predecessor term called ALTE (Apparent Life-Threatening Event) was studied partly because doctors wondered whether it might be linked to SIDS. However, research over time found that most of these events were not precursors to SIDS , which led the American Academy of Pediatrics to replace ALTE with the more specific term BRUE in 2016.

"There was no reason for why it happened," Wells said. "Nothing clogged her airways. Her heart was healthy. Her oxygen levels were fine. Overall, she seemed healthy on all of her scans."

Though Wells administered CPR to Stevie at the time, she later realized she had done so "incorrectly." Nevertheless, it had the desired effect, with Wells saying doctors told her that "if it ever happens again, do exactly what you did."

The incident has haunted Wells ever since.

"It's by far the most gut-wrenching, horrible, nauseating experience I've ever lived through," she said. "I had a glimpse of what it would feel like to lose her, and I now have 10 seconds of a pain I'll forever be terrified to feel again."

There are still nights when she struggles to sleep with Stevie nearby.

"I just sit there and watch her breathe," she said. "Sometimes her breathing slows down and I go into immediate panic mode."

Wells hopes her story inspires other parents to learn infant CPR.

"You never think you're actually going to need to use it until suddenly you do, and in that moment you don't have time to Google what to do or second-guess yourself," she said.

However, she also believes she got "incredibly lucky" that morning.

"I happened to find my daughter when I did, I was able to react, and thankfully what I did worked," she said.

"I never want another parent to hear my story and think that if they had just checked one more time, known CPR better, or done something differently, their outcome would have been different. Sometimes parents do everything right and still experience an unimaginable loss. That is not a failure on their part."

articles.summary: Major Jason Watson faces charges under rarely-used military law prohibiting criticism of the US president.
articles.body:
The United States Air Force said it is seeking charges under the military justice system against Major Jason Watson for his public call for the impeachment and removal from office of President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance over the US-Israel war on Iran.

“Major Watson acted knowing the ⁠risks to his career and his liberty,” ⁠Watson’s lawyer Christopher Mutimer said on Tuesday. “It is my hope that other Americans who feel powerless in this moment will take some measure of courage ⁠from his willingness to speak and to stand by his convictions.”

Watson, an active-duty officer, was detained by police in his uniform in July on the steps of the US Capitol, where he had taken part in a protest holding a sign calling for Trump and Vance to be removed from office. The protest, which was also attended by US lawmakers, was organised by activists from the group Removal Coalition, which said at the time that Watson was the “first active duty officer in the military to call for Trump’s impeachment and removal from office”.

Watson appeared earlier this month on CNN, where he again called for the removal of Trump, who, as president, serves as the commander in chief of the military.

“What is happening with President Trump is not normal. He has failed us,” Watson said. “And not only is he a failure as president; he is flagrantly violating the Constitution, breaking the law, engaged in rampant corruption and is killing Americans. And that is unacceptable to me, and it should be unacceptable to all of us.”

On Tuesday, Watson’s lawyer said in a statement that the airman would face charges under three articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, including Article 88 – a rarely used provision which accuses him of using “contemptuous words against the President, the Vice President, Congress”.

The Air ⁠Force confirmed Watson had been charged ⁠and said he would continue to be held in pre-trial confinement and be afforded the right to due process.

articles.title: Cyclosporiasis cases in US climb to 17,180, CDC says
articles.summary: Aug 25 () - The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Tuesday reported 17,180 confirmed ‌cases of cyclosporiasis in the United States, ‌an increase o...
articles.body:
Aug 25 (Reuters) - The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Tuesday reported 17,180 confirmed ‌cases of cyclosporiasis in the United States, ‌an increase of 1,464 cases from a week ago.

• The CDC said it has received reports of 17,180 confirmed cases across 48 states plus the District of Columbia, with 922 hospitalizations and two deaths ‌as of August 24. ⁠At least 11,844 additional cases may require further investigation and analysis, CDC said.

• ⁠The data include the cases reported in the ongoing multistate outbreak linked to recalled iceberg lettuce, CDC ​said, adding ​that it is investigating ​multiple clusters of cyclosporiasis.

• ‌CDC and FDA are investigating at least six other clusters for which sources have not yet been confirmed, CDC said.

• Michigan, the hardest-hit state, logged a slow 3% rise to 14,277 last week, hinting ‌the outbreak may be easing.

• ​The cyclosporiasis outbreak is one ​of the largest foodborne ​illness events in recent U.S. history. ‌The illness is caused by ​the cyclospora ​parasite, which can lead to diarrhea, nausea and other gastrointestinal symptoms.

• The outbreak has shaken U.S. ​consumers nationwide, causing ‌many to forgo eating fresh produce or ​dining in restaurants.

(Reporting by Christy Santhosh in Bengaluru; ​Editing by Vijay Kishore)

There was no official briefing on the decisions of the Cabinet meeting chaired by PM Narendra Modi.In Jan, railway board chairperson Satish Kumar had said the project cost had increased by around 83% to Rs 1.98 lakh crore. articles.title: Expert witnesses challenge claim that Lindsay Clancy experienced psychosis
articles.summary: One more day of testimony expected as closing arguments set for Thursday and jury likely begins deliberations Friday
articles.body:
One more day of rebuttal testimony was expected this week in the trial against Lindsay Clancy, followed by closing statements likely on Thursday.

The jury, which will likely begin deliberations on Friday, will decide whether the Massachusetts mother was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed her three children in January 2023.

On Tuesday, prosecutors put two expert witnesses on the stand who challenged the arguments made by Clancy's defense team – specifically, that Clancy committed the acts while suffering from postpartum psychosis – a mental illness that can cause hallucinations, mood swings, delusions and more, and was hearing a voice compelling her to do it. Her attorney Kevin Reddington has also claimed Clancy had bipolar disorder and was overmedicated.

Tuesday's testimonies capped off more than a month of testimony in a trial that has largely depended on opposing views from experts about Clancy's mental health and her ability to understand the gravity of what she was doing. It's not disputed that she strangled the children – Callan, 8 months, Dawson, three years old, and Cora, five years old, before she allegedly jumped from a second-floor window, which left her paralyzed from the waist down. But the outcome of the trial hinges on questions surrounding Clancy's mental state at the time of the children's deaths. The burden of proof is on the prosecution to show Clancy was not suffering from "a mental disease or defect" and that she had enough capacity to understand "the wrongfulness or criminality of her conduct".

Kirk Heilbrun, a forensic psychologist hired by prosecutors, initially took the stand on Friday and continued his testimony on Tuesday morning. He told the court he "did his best to have an open mind", when he evaluated Clancy in April and that he believed she was "criminally responsible" for the deaths.

Related: Lindsay Clancy trial: psychologist says he doubts claim she was hallucinating

"She retained an awareness of the illegality of killing others, including her children," he said. "Her moral awareness of this killing was influenced by her strong desire to die and, if she was dead, not to leave her children behind."

Over nearly three days of testimony, the prosecution also focused on the timeline of events during the killings, asking Heilbrun to identify whether each step Clancy took was a decision – including her action to take the children down to the basement – in an attempt to convince the jury that these were planned murders. For each, he answered that they did.

Under cross-examination, Heilbrun's told the court he had been paid roughly $54,000 for the 180 hours he has worked on the case on behalf of the state, and that he will likely be paid more as the trial goes on. He also told Reddington that he didn't have experience with postpartum mental health conditions.

A recess was called at one point, after several heated exchanges between Heilbrun and Reddington during which Clancy's attorney accused the psychologist of not reading her medical reports.

Heilbrun's testimony on Monday prompted a request for a mistrial from Reddington after the psychologist mentioned Clancy's Catholic faith. The request was denied, but Judge William Sullivan admonished Heilbrun for the comment and instructed the jury to disregard the reference to "the religion that the defendant was raised with", calling it "an absolutely inappropriate area of testimony".

After Heilbrun left the stand on Tuesday afternoon, prosecutors called forensic psychiatrist Gregory Saathoff, who is affiliated with the FBI and University of Virginia. Unlike Heilbrun, he claimed he was not paid for his testimony and had treated several women who have killed their children.

Saathoff told the court that it was unusual that Clancy hadn't reported hearing voices before the killings and that the voices ceased afterwards. He also said he found several inconsistencies in Clancy's account of what happened.

It is well documented that Clancy needed treatment for a mental health condition, and admitted herself to McLean, a psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts, a few weeks before the murders. Testimony from expert witnesses who were called by the defense had very different conclusions about her mental state.

Dr Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist and expert in filicide, testified on Friday that Clancy was "clearly psychotic" on the day she killed her children and was not in control of her actions.

"It was almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings," he said.

That echoed another defense witness, Paul Zeizel, the psychologist who concluded Clancy "had no appreciation for the wrongfulness of her act".

Before the court adjourned for the day on Tuesday, Judge Sullivan told the jury that the presentation of evidence would conclude on Wednesday and that closing arguments would likely follow on Thursday. Deliberations are expected to begin on Friday. He encouraged jurors not to form their own conclusions until the very end.

"You've heard a lot of evidence, but you haven't heard all of it, right? And like I said before, you haven't heard the closing arguments of the attorneys," Sullivan said. "You haven't heard the law that you're going to have to apply to this. So you still have to keep an open mind."

articles.title: Massachusetts cuts Flock ties, seeks charges after officer accused of tracking ex-girlfriend
articles.summary: "Using that access for a personal purpose is a serious violation of that trust, and it is a crime."
articles.body:
An automated license plate reader program in Stow, Massachusetts, is being dismantled after investigators said a police officer used law enforcement databases for personal reasons.

The Lowell Sun reported that officer Jason Rogers, who served as a detective and acting sergeant, is facing both termination proceedings and potential criminal charges.

Town officials said Rogers obtained information about someone identified as his former girlfriend. Police said the matter began June 18, when a complaint was filed.

The paper noted that Rogers was placed on paid administrative leave within three hours and stripped of access to department systems.

Police said the internal affairs inquiry found that several database searches had no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Investigators counted at least five instances in which Rogers accessed Criminal Offender Record Information through the Criminal Justice Information Services system, along with vehicle searches run on multiple dates.

"Law enforcement officers are entrusted with access to sensitive information solely so they can perform their official duties and protect the public," Police Chief Michael Sallese told the Sun. "Using that access for a personal purpose is a serious violation of that trust, and it is a crime."

The department said the investigation found several violations, including database policy breaches, false or unsubstantiated search reasons, failure to comply with written orders, misuse of official position, and conduct unbecoming an officer.

The paper reported that Stow officials removed the last Flock automated license plate reader still operating in the town because of the incident.

Before using similar technology again, the Stow Police Department told the Sun it needs stronger safeguards, clearer rules, and better oversight. Even though plate reader data has helped solve crimes and locate missing people, its misuse is sparking nationwide backlash.

When used correctly, tools such as camera networks, automated searches, and large-scale data systems can help optimize traffic flow, improve public services, and support cleaner energy systems by helping utilities balance electricity demand.

At the same time, AI-related computing can consume large amounts of electricity and water, strain the power grid, and create security and privacy risks when used in the wrong way.

Following the investigation, the Stow Police Department sent the matter to the Middlesex County District Attorney's Office in order to seek charges.

Sallese also provided the full internal affairs report to the Massachusetts Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission, which the Sun said could decide what action to take regarding Rogers' certification to work as a police officer.

At the policy level, Sallese plans to bring a revised plate reader policy to the Select Board for future consideration. Officials said it would define when the technology could be used, require supervisory approval before use, and impose extensive logging and reporting requirements.

"The actions of one individual do not represent the values or conduct we expect from the good and dedicated members of the Stow Police Department," Town Administrator Denise M. Dembkoski told the paper.

articles.title: Report kept from residents now revealed, shows toxic levels in East Palestine
articles.summary: East Palestine residents participating in a class-action settlement say lawyers suppressed their expert’s environmental report to convince them to take the m...
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Shortly after the 2023 train derailment and burning of vinyl chloride in East Palestine, Ohio, renowned exposure-warnings expert and industrial hygienist Stephen Petty tested the soil and water for residents.

Petty had been hired by class-action attorneys as their testing expert.

When the attorneys negotiated a $600 million settlement with Norfolk Southern , they did not release Petty's results — even to their own clients.

Nexstar's NewsNation has obtained those results and interviewed Petty.

Never-released report shows contamination, Petty says

Petty told NewsNation there are carcinogens in the soil in East Palestine and that they are "above screening levels, which means you can't walk away from it."

Petty said his testing data, and other data he analyzed, show dioxins and PAHs ( polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons ), some of the most carcinogenic compounds on the planet, at elevated levels.

The levels are above cancer-screening levels set by the EPA , which requires further testing and analysis.

"Somewhere between 50% and 70% of the data points, whether they be for dioxins or PAHs, exceeded screening levels" for cancer, Petty said.

"You have to do something. You have to do further analysis to see what needs to be done from a remediation standpoint. And you also have to do further analysis to determine what it means for people in that environment," Petty said. "There is a problem there."

Independent testing expert Scott Smith also came to test on his own. He said he found elevated levels of dioxin, too. Smith and Petty are both whistleblowers represented by the Government Accountability Project.

"It's astounding in that it was suppressed," he said. "Forty-nine percent of the testing exceeds the EPA cancer screening level. Seventy percent of Stephen Petty's data and analysis shows polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons above the EPA cancer screening level."

"It lines up exactly with my data," he said.

Their own lawyers kept the data from them, residents say

Residents said the story they got from the attorneys in the class-action lawsuit was very different.

"Petty's test results were always really secret," East Palestine resident Beth Kosar said. "They said it would hurt the case."

"They told me that in my home, basically, that the numbers didn't support the outcome of the $600 million," resident Linda Murphy said. "The numbers weren't bad enough. And if they revealed them to the court, the $600 million may not even go through because the contamination levels were not bad enough. There would be no long-term health effects risks."

Murphy shared an audio recording she said was from a meeting with the lawyers. In the recording, the speakers can be heard saying, "The data is nowhere near as bad as we thought it was going to be when this first happened."

The speaker also said, "It's almost unprovably bad, specifically for medical monitoring, showing that people have been exposed at a certain level so as to require 10, 20 years of diagnostic testing. Virtually unprovable for any long-term chronic future illness like cancer."

They also said, "The chemicals did not persist long enough at quantities that will expose people over the necessary period of time to produce long-term health effects that are associated directly to this exposure."

Austin Druckenbrod, another East Palestine resident, said he asked the lawyers directly about the tests: "I asked him when I was concerned about the testing they had, that it may not have been the truth. And he said, 'They're hacks. And Scott Smith doesn't know what he's talking about. And neither does Stephen Petty,' And he said, 'Don't believe them.'"

NewsNation has reviewed text messages that appear to back up what Druckenbrod told us.

Though the attorneys didn't share Petty's results with residents, they did enlist a toxicologist to film a video that played for the residents.

The video was filmed by Dr. Arch "Chip" Carson, M.D., PhD., who is listed on the video as principal of Environmental Medicine Consultants. He is associated with multiple universities, including Ohio State University , the University of Cincinnati and the University of Texas School of Public Health.

In one part of the video, Dr. Carson said, "The levels that people were exposed to in the community were so small that we don't expect any kinds of cancers or health effects to have resulted from those. There will not be any long-term health impact of chemical exposure from the derailment to community members of East Palestine."

Petty told NewsNation, "The argument that there is nothing to see here is factually false. Multiple people saying there's nothing to see here … are just flat out lying or are wrong."

Mindy Bish is an attorney now representing East Palestine residents who are trying to rescind their participation in the settlement.

"Arch Carson told everyone that there was, that he would expect no cancers as a result of this exposure. No cancers. And there are cancers developing almost every week in East Palestine and someone dying of cancer almost every month," Bish told NewsNation.

"These attorneys told them that the Stephen Petty information would not support the claims. And that is not true," Bish said. "My first impressions when I saw Stephen Petty's results was this is fraudulent, this is concealment, this is manipulation."

Neither Carson nor the attorneys in the class-action settlement have responded to requests for comment from NewsNation.

Nearly 90 residents are seeking to rescind their participation in the settlement.

In part, their motion alleged "Substantial evidence of fraud and misrepresentation by class counsel, who concealed critical expert findings about health risks while inducing class members to sign personal injury releases in exchange for inadequate personal injury payments."

In April, a judge denied their effort to reopen the settlement. They have filed an appeal alleging that class counsel's own expert, Petty, held opinions materially adverse to the settlement that were not disclosed before opt-in.

"I believe I was manipulated," Druckenbord said. "I believe there was fraud. And I have the future, and my future is going to rely on proving the bad actors were wrong."

articles.title: Seven killed in Gaza as Israeli strike ‘destroys’ aid supply warehouse
articles.summary: Health Ministry warns of ‘complete collapse of the basic necessities of life’ in Gaza as Israel’s attacks continue.
articles.body:
Israeli strikes have killed at least seven Palestinians across Gaza, according to local medical sources, in ongoing violations of a "ceasefire" that went into effect last October.

Three Palestinians were killed and others injured in a strike on a home in Beit Lahiya, near Kamal Adwan Hospital, on Tuesday, a source at al-Shifa Hospital said.

Earlier in the day, a drone strike that hit a gathering of civilians killed a man in Khan Younis's al-Mawasi area, and injured three others.

Three other Palestinians died from wounds they sustained in earlier Israeli raids on Khan Younis, said Al Jazeera Arabic correspondent Nour Khaled.

Two of them died from injuries suffered in an attack on Monday, while the third had been wounded about two weeks ago, she said.

An Israeli military strike overnight into Tuesday also destroyed a warehouse storing nutrition supplies intended for children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers in Gaza, Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) said.

"The force of the explosion caused large sections of the building to collapse, including the roof and walls, completely burying supplies beneath the rubble," MAP said in a statement.

"Humanitarian workers, humanitarian facilities and the supplies that people depend on must be protected," it added.

The warehouse belongs to Ard El Insan (AEI), a local humanitarian organisation working with MAP to support about 60 medical points serving up to 100 women and children daily.

The overnight explosion collapsed large sections of the building, including the roof and walls, burying the supplies under rubble, according to MAP, which said the entire stock was damaged and rendered unfit for human consumption.

"Losing these quantities in their entirety is a major blow to our work and will undoubtedly affect our ability to reach the children and women who need these services, particularly given the conditions they continue to face in the aftermath of starvation," said Sahar Salem, AEI's project coordinator.

"Even with the ceasefire, conditions on the ground remain extremely challenging, and children and women still urgently need continued support, she added.

She said two of her colleagues have been killed and another wounded since Israel's genocidal war on Gaza began.

Also on Tuesday, the head of Gaza's Ministry of Health warned of "complete collapse of the basic necessities of life" amid critical oxygen supply shortages.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Director-General Dr Munir al-Bursh said that Israel "continues to escalate its attacks on Gaza and violate the ceasefire agreement, which is present in statements but absent from people's lives on the ground".

Al-Bursh added that "only 12 oxygen stations remain operational out of around 34", and warned that "any additional breakdown could cut off oxygen to patients".

"If this oxygen supply stops, these people will die," he said. "We do not want to reach the point where a doctor is forced to choose between two patients, deciding who receives oxygen and who is left without it."

Ongoing Israeli attacks and ceasefire violations come despite US President Donald Trump's call for Israel to halt its attacks.

In an interview with Fox News on August 17, Trump said that Israel "should not be striking in Gaza", and that "Hamas agreed to lay down their weapons" under the terms of a US-backed peace plan.

articles.title: A Pittsburgh school went from 130 fights per year to 10, using an idea from ‘Harry Potter’
articles.summary: A school in Pittsburgh nearly eliminated its violence problem by, in part, implementing a school house system a la Harry Potter.
articles.body:
Pittsburgh Arlington PreK-8 public school had a major behavior problem on its hands. With just 360 students enrolled, the school saw more than 130 fights in the 2024-25 school year. Many of the kids who weren't suspended for violence were chronically absent.

The school also couldn't hold on to a principal , going through four in just a couple of years.

Finally, school leadership decided to take action.

Principal and staff begin making major changes

Principal Crystal Caldwell and her leadership staff knew they had to do something. The reputation of the school had reached rock bottom.

"Arlington's history has been a school of violence, and 'Oh, don't send your kid there,'" she told TribLive .

Step one was increasing communication. Caldwell and supporting staff began having "safety huddles" every morning with teachers in order to identify potential conflicts before they exploded into physical fights.

Some days that might mean pulling an irritable student aside for counseling or keeping a watchful eye out for kids who are showing signs of struggling at home. All of the staff banded together to keep these little problems from boiling over.

They also began leaning into a concept known as "restorative practices." Whenever possible, it replaces traditional punishments like detention and suspension with actions that help repair the harm the student caused in the school community. A student might have to clean the hallway if they vandalized it, or apologize and talk it out when they've had a conflict with another student.

"We let the kids talk it out, and they come up with their own way to apologize and say how they will do better," Caldwell told TribLive. "They need a moment of knowing it's OK to make mistakes, but knowing they can learn from it."

But perhaps the most interesting change Caldwell and her team enacted was ripped right out of the pages of Harry Potter .

Harry Potter -inspired 'house' system builds community among students

In Harry Potter , students at the magical wizarding school of Hogwarts are sorted into houses upon their arrival—Hufflepuff, Slytherin, Ravenclaw, and of course, Gryffindor. It's like a little team with its very own mascot, virtues, and color scheme. Students can earn or lose points for their house throughout the year in an epic competition with the other houses.

It's an idea taken from real-life British boarding schools , and it's now making its way into American public schools as evidenced by Pittsburgh Arlington.

The house system builds community and belonging for students. Competing against the other houses via good behavior also creates a built-in reward system that the students love.

After 130 fights at Pittsburgh Arlington in 2024, last school year there were only 10. That's right, just 10 fights after implementing safety huddles, the house system, and other changes. That's an absolutely incredible turnaround for a school that was on the brink.

House system is making a difference in schools all over the country

Houses have been so effective in Pittsburgh that the public school district is now rolling the program out to dozens of schools.

It's also being used in nearby Duquesne City Schools where the district has reported a 74% drop in student disciplinary incidents since implementing houses.

Union County public schools in North Carolina are utilizing a similar system at about a dozen elementary schools. And that's not even including the many individual schools around the country that are taking matters into their own hands to try out the clever idea from the wizarding world.

There are a lot of mechanisms hidden inside the house system that make it incredibly effective at engaging students. For starters, all kids find a sense of belonging and loyalty to their house just by the simple act of being sorted. Students are sorted into houses across different grades, so a natural mentorship arrangement often arises where older students can help younger students. Positive, pro-social behavior also becomes gamified via friendly competition.

Having a house system has been shown to reduce bullying, lower the number of fights and suspensions, and even improve academic performance across the board.

When students are experiencing homelessness or extreme poverty, violence in the streets on which they live, hunger, and more, they often act out and struggle in school.

But along with other schools around the country, Pittsburgh Arlington is proving that it's still possible to make school a safe, welcoming place even when the world outside is anything but—and that can make all the difference.

articles.title: Syrian Kurdish leader dissolves force that spearheaded jihadist fight
articles.summary: The leader of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, the Washington-backed group at the forefront of the battle against the Islamic State jihadist group,...
articles.body:
The leader of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, the Washington-backed group at the forefront of the battle against the Islamic State jihadist group, announced their dissolution on Tuesday under a deal with the government.

After being Syria's most highly trained and organised paramilitary force for years, the SDF was promptly dropped by Washington in favour of the new US-friendly authorities in Damascus after the ousting of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in late 2024.

The forces' leader, Mazloum Abdi, declared their dissolution in a televised speech at the presidential palace in Damascus.

"We announce today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and declare, with full responsibility, their dissolution as an independent military force," he said.

Abdi explained that the announcement followed "the completion of the process of integrating our forces into the brigades of the Syrian army".

The SDF was formed in 2015 at the instigation of the United States, which was impressed by the Kurdish fighters who had defeated IS in Kobane in the north and was seeking a reliable partner in the ongoing battle against the jihadists.

The group went on to spearhead the battle against IS, which was defeated territorially in Syria four years later.

The US special envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, hailed the group's disbandment on Tuesday.

"This is what real integration looks like: not winners and losers, but former counterparts with differing points of view crafting a diplomatic solution to strengthen the sovereign nation of Syria. One army, one government, one state," said Barrack, who is also Washington's ambassador to Turkey.

"Since the creation of the SDF, its fighters have shouldered a heavy responsibility during one of the most difficult periods" for Syria, Abdi said in his address.

"They liberated many Syrian cities and towns, first from the Baathist regime, then from the terrorism of Daesh," he continued, using the Arabic acronym for IS.

"The circumstances have changed today and the country has entered a new phase characterised by peace and participation."

The SDF amassed around 100,000 fighters at its peak, both Kurds and Arabs, and controlled swathes of Syria's oil-rich north and northeast.

But following January clashes that saw the Kurds lose large chunks of territory to government troops, the two sides signed a deal to integrate Kurdish military and civilian institutions into the state.

During the violence, Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa signed a decree enshrining the Kurds' national rights and recognising Kurdish as a national language, an unprecedented step since Syria's independence in 1946.

Arabs within the SDF's ranks also defected en masse after Sharaa's army took control of two previously Kurdish-held provinces, Raqa and Deir Ezzor, leaving them at half their strength, according to Syria specialist Fabrice Balanche.

The Kurdish force faced repeated Turkish invasions between 2016 and 2019, with Ankara saying it wanted to push the fighters away from its border.

Turkey has long viewed the SDF as linked to the militant Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which waged a decades-long insurgency in the country.

The January agreement, under which Kurdish fighters would be integrated into state structures, stipulates that the SDF commit to expelling all non-Syrian PKK leaders and members from the country.

The SDF's integration into the state is a major victory for Sharaa, who has been trying to cement control over all of Syria since Assad's fall.

However, the deal represented the last nail in the coffin for the Kurds' long-held dream of autonomy.

Last week, Abdi announced that the integration of the Kurdish administration with the Syrian state was complete, adding: "Our struggle will continue, to cement our people's rights in the constitution."

articles.title: US judge blocks Ohio law requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote
articles.summary: The amended law was an attempt by state Republicans to crack down on unproven claims of voting by noncitizens.
articles.body:
A United States federal court has temporarily blocked an Ohio law that required proof of US citizenship from residents who wanted to register to vote while they obtained a driver’s license.

In his ruling on Tuesday, US District Judge Solomon Oliver Jr granted a preliminary injunction against the law, saying it likely violates the US National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) because it requires more information than necessary to determine a resident’s eligibility to vote.

“Election officials do not need documentary proof of citizenship to assess a voter registration applicant’s citizenship because signed attestation of citizenship is enough,” Oliver wrote.

The judge also pointed to a clause in the act that says each US state’s driver’s license application “shall serve as an application for voter registration with respect to election for Federal office unless the applicant fails to sign the voter registration application”.

Oliver said that Ohio must offer applicants the opportunity to register once they’ve submitted their driver’s license application, not after it’s been approved by the state’s Bureau of Motor Vehicles (BMV).

“To interpret this section of the NVRA otherwise would allow States to make registering to vote at the BMV more onerous, and could result in fewer voter registrations because the opportunity to apply was not proactively offered to otherwise eligible citizens,” Oliver added.

In 1995, Ohio passed a so-called “motor-voter” law that allowed residents the opportunity to register to vote when they applied for a driver’s license

But that law was amended last year by the state’s Republican-controlled legislature in an attempt to crack down on unproven claims, pushed in part by US President Donald Trump, that noncitizens were voting in the state’s election. US law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections.

The ruling marks a victory for voting rights advocates like Red Wine & Blue, which sued Ohio’s secretary of state, Frank LaRose, over claims that the law disenfranchised eligible voters and violated the NVRA.

One of the group’s lawyers, Ben Stafford, praised the ruling, calling it “a win for Ohio voters.”

“With the registration deadline just weeks away, eligible Ohioans will now have the opportunity to register to vote at the BMV without having to produce unnecessary paperwork that is not required by federal law,” Stafford, an attorney at Elias Law Group, said in a statement.

LaRose said his office disagrees with the decision and will appeal.

articles.title: Canada unveils counter-tariffs of 15-50% on US goods
articles.summary: Canada on Tuesday announced counter-tariffs on US goods ranging between 15 and 50 percent, intensifying the trade war between the historically close allies.T...
articles.body:
Canada on Tuesday announced counter-tariffs on US goods ranging between 15 and 50 percent, intensifying the trade war between the historically close allies.

Ottawa's retaliation will take effect September 8, a timeframe earlier outlined by Prime Minister Mark Carney after US President Donald Trump's 50-percent duties came into place Saturday.

The retaliatory tariffs of 15 percent, 25 percent or 50 percent match US levels, said Canada's Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne. They impact industries including steel, dairy and electronics.

The list includes frozen and fresh fish, consumer goods like dishwashers and washing machines, as well as industrial products including railway construction materials.

Canada's government also announced a $5.4 billion (CA$7.5 billion) aid package for firms and workers.

"This is an unprecedented challenge imposed on Canada. But Canada will meet the moment," Champagne added. "I think what Canadians can see this morning is that we stand united."

Industry Minister Melanie Joly echoed Champagne's call for Canadians to support local businesses, vowing to work with new allies and trading partners.

She also pledged to "fight back" if Trump raised US tariffs on Canadian autos to 50 percent.

Trump's latest tariffs hit about $20 billion in Canadian goods -- or 5.5 percent of its exports to the United States -- after trade negotiations collapsed at the eleventh hour.

Under Canada's planned response, US steel and aluminum products previously subject to a 25-percent duty will soon face 50-percent tariffs.

Goods facing 25-percent tariffs include appliances, dairy products like cheese, as well as certain steel and aluminum derivative products.

A small category will see a 15-percent duty, including electric equipment and tools.

These form about 7.3 percent of Canada's imports from the United States at 2024 levels.

But analysts warn of tit-for-tat escalation.

Already on Monday, Trump pledged to double tariffs on Canadian autos starting 2027, up to 50 percent from the current 25 percent for non-US content.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford criticized Trump's threat, saying he could "kiss my ass" and threatening an electricity export surcharge.

Trump lashed out at Ford and also referred to Carney as a "governor," re-upping his inflammatory push for Canada to become the 51st US state.

Highlighting the animosity, Trump said Tuesday he was considering renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

The fresh US tariffs do not exempt products under the US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement. They raise the US effective tariff rate on Canadian exports to 6.9 percent from 5.1 percent, Oxford Economics estimates.

Tariffs on plastics, electrical machinery, and wood and paper products contribute most to the increase.

"Manufacturers in Quebec, New Brunswick, and Ontario will be affected the most," Oxford Economics said.

The exchanges drew some concern in the United States. Ethan Johnson, 25, who runs a start-up, told AFP: "The economics and the math behind it do not make sense."

But 29-year-old electrician Lucas Feser trusts the Trump administration "to set up a harder, better deal."

Carney previously said US negotiators sought restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the last minute.

US officials made unacceptable "threats" to the French language and "Quebec culture" too, he added, referring to eastern Canada's French-speaking province.

Trump pushed back Tuesday, saying on Truth Social that he would "never interfere with Canadians speaking French." He accused Carney of lying for political support.

The United States is Canada's biggest trading partner. Canadian exports to its neighbor represent 70 percent of its overall total.

Canada is the second-biggest US trading partner in goods this year behind Mexico.

Polling released Sunday by the Angus Reid Institute showed Canadians broadly support Carney's move to walk away from talks, but some fear economic repercussions.

The White House had alleged "discriminatory treatment" by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in rolling out new tariffs.

articles.title: Florida tourism sees decline as Canadians skip visits amid Trump trade war
articles.summary: The Canadian tourism slump has the hospitality industry worried across multiple states
articles.body:
Tourism from Canada to the U.S. has been impacted across the country amid the Trump administration's ongoing trade war with its traditional ally.

In Florida, tourism from Canada was down more than four percent in the second quarter of this year, compared with the same period in 2025.

In the first six months of this year, Canadian tourism to the Sunshine State was down nearly 14 percent, according to Visit Florida .

The drop comes as the Trump administration has spent months antagonizing Canada, typically a staunch U.S. ally and major trading partner.

The White House has launched 50 percent tariffs on Canadian products, and Canada has responded with retaliatory measures, further souring a relationship already under strain from the president's repeated suggestions the country could become the 51st state .

Researchers in Canada have identified a similar decline.

Canadian visits to U.S. metro areas fell by about 42 percent since Trump took office, experts at the University of Toronto found by analyzing cell phone data. Six of the 10 cities that have seen the largest decline in visitors from Canada were in Florida, according to the researchers, though Myrtle Beach, South Carolina topped the list.

Overall, border crossings into the U.S. from Canada were down by more than a quarter in 2025, compared with 2024, according to the Canadian government .

"Excluding the COVID-19 pandemic period, the resulting 11-month streak of year-over-year declines was the deepest and most sustained on record for border crossings from the United States," Statistics Canada wrote in July, comparing the drop in travel to the months after the 9/11 terror attack in New York City.

The impact has been felt in major tourist destinations across the country.

In Las Vegas, visits from Canada were down about 18 percent in 2025.

This August, city tourism officials went on a sales mission in Western Canada to bolster demand.

"We're here to make sure you know that we care about Canada," Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority CEO Steve Hill said at a kickoff event. "We know that Canada loves Las Vegas. We love Canada right back!"

In New York, meanwhile, Canadian tourism was down 26 percent in 2025 compared to the previous year, while spending from these tourists was down 14 percent from pre-pandemic levels.

"Our tourism economy cannot afford another year of trade wars with Canada that drive away our most important international visitors," Vijay Dandapani, president and CEO of the Hotel Association of New York City, told The City Reporter. "The federal government must reach a deal with Canada and give travelers a reason to come back. If we fail to act, New York risks losing even more visitors from our number one tourism partner."

articles.title: ‘There will never be another Dolly’: Tributes to Parton pour in across generations
articles.summary: Entertainers and celebrities reflected on Parton’s creative talent, while fans and everyday people recounted how her philanthropic generosity touched their lives.
articles.body: Reflecting the magnitude of her influence and impact, Dolly Parton’s death drew immediate tributes from across industries, genres, generations, places and people. Entertainers, film stars, politicians and everyday people who benefited from her generosity and her enterprises quickly filled social media with their stories of how she improved their lives, how her songs uplifted or taught them, how she made them laugh and how they just loved who she was. The accolades poured in from around the globe, offered up from sources as varied as country music superstars Reba McEntire, Kacey Musgraves and Linda Ronstadt to Khloe Kardashian and the Muppets, as well as singers and other celebrities, including Mick Jagger, Dionne Warwick, Pink, Keke Palmer, Lily Tomlin, Kelly Clarkson, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and fashion designer Donatella Versace. President Donald Trump ordered flags lowered for a week, writing on Truth Social, “There has never been anyone like her, and there never will,” as politicians from both sides of the aisle paid tribute. Former President Bill Clinton wrote on social media that Parton was “one of a kind — a great songwriter and performer who told the stories of everyday Americans with honesty, humility, and heart. She rose high from her East Tennessee roots and never forgot where she came from.” McEntire wrote of getting the news that “my buddy Dolly passed onto the higher and greater side.” She thanked her for “all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth” and said, “There will never ever be another you.” Some of country music’s royalty sang her praises and were joined by a younger generation of musicians and songwriters who heralded her as an inspiration. “This really hurts,” wrote Musgraves, a multiple Grammy award winner. Parton drew an homage from the “King of Country Music,” George Strait, who said on Facebook: “You’ve had such a huge impact all over the world, @dollyparton. We will all miss you. May God bless the Parton family.” The adoration was not confined to country music. “She was a sweet and kind soul and I’m proud to say I knew her. ... There will never be another Dolly,” said Gene Simmons, bassist and co-founder of the hard rock band Kiss. The Muppets posted a black-and-white photo of Parton with Miss Piggy, saying, “She filled the world with light and we are so grateful for every second we got to spend with her onstage and off.” Comedian Lily Tomlin, Parton’s longtime friend, wrote, “No words...” followed by a broken heart emoji, alongside a black-and-white photo of the two, side by side with large smiles. In a video reel, Tomlin featured photos of herself with Jane Fonda, who co-starred with them in the 1980s hit “9 to 5.” Parton’s title song for the 1980 movie — which topped the Billboard country chart — played in the background. National Organization for Women President Kim Villanueva said in a statement that Parton “defined feminism,” adding that her role in “9 to 5” emphasized that women in the workplace “deserved to be treated equally and with respect.” “She encouraged women to embrace who they wanted to be and stand up for their values,” Villanueva wrote. Donna Brazile, the former chair of the Democratic National Convention, posted that Parton “spent decades quietly funding band uniforms and instruments at Black high schools across the South — never once putting her name on it. No headlines, no fanfare — just help, given because it was needed.” Meanwhile, Rep. Tim Burchett, a Republican from Tennessee, Parton’s native state, said the state had lost one of its greatest ambassadors, who represented “the very best of the American dream.” Parton’s music “inspired generations of Americans and her philanthropic work helped provide greater access to education for countless young Tennesseans,” he said. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., wrote on X, “Rest in peace, Dolly Parton — a true legend and a force for good.” Parton’s Dollywood Foundation focused on improving children’s educational success and stemming dropout rates in Tennessee. It gave birth to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, which sent books to children around the world. Her work was inspired by her father’s illiteracy. A father who said he’s in Australia posted on X that his young daughter got her first book Monday night from Parton’s Imagination Library. All of his children read it with their mother and laughed and enjoyed it, he said. The Library of Congress posted a photo of Parton, with reading glasses, conducting a story time book reading to children at the library. It described her as a “titan of children’s literacy” and said she donated the 100 millionth book to its collection. Parton helped fund crucial infectious disease research, with Scientific American paying tribute to her for her $1 million donation to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee, to help fund an early-stage trial of the Covid vaccine in 2020. She told NBC News that she donated to the vaccine effort because “I just wanted to do good.” She also helped promote Covid vaccinations with a video of her getting the shot and an adjustment to her song “Jolene” to “Vaccine.” The Motion Picture Academy awarded her its Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award last year. Dollywood, Parton’s much-beloved theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, will open Wednesday. “In her spirit, Dollywood will be open Wednesday as Dolly wanted, always reminding everyone with her signature sparkle — ‘the show must go on,’” the company said in a statement. “Together, we honor her by carrying forward her message of love, perseverance and hope.”
